abstract:
  "The Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) decomposes response time and accuracy data from speeded decision-making tasks into cognitive process parameters. Despite its success, DDM analyses still often rely on step-wise procedures that fit each participant separately and test point estimates afterwards, which discards uncertainty and invites over-parametrization. In part this is done due to the computational complexity, the difficulty of specifying hierarchical models for DDMs, and the time it takes to run parameter estimation. The bmm R package implements one-step Bayesian hierarchical estimation of DDM parameters through three approaches: the EZ-Diffusion Model, which works from summary statistics and fits in minutes; the Censored-Shifted Wald; and full DDM likelihood estimation via the Wiener first-passage time distribution. This tutorial centers on the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model and shows that it evaluates condition effects on the four main DDM parameters quick and accurately. Across three tutorials the approaches are applied to the classic lexical decision dataset of Wagenmakers et al. (2008); On this data set, every condition effect tested using the EZ-Diffusion approach aligned with estimation using the full DDM, at a fraction of the computational cost; the absolute values of boundary separation and non-decision time differed between approaches. Additionally, a parameter recovery study demonstrates what the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model recovers when the starting point is biased; and the trial-level approaches are fitted at the same specification for comparison. The tutorial also introduces the preprocessing tools bmm provides for handling contaminant responses. Complete R scripts accompany every tutorial. After working through the tutorials, readers will be able to preprocess RT data, fit the EZ-Diffusion Model as a primary analysis, and decide when a trial-level approach is needed."

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, rtdists, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork)
source(here("functions", "clean_plot.R"))

# --- Helpers -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Format estimate with 95% CrI
fmt_est <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sprintf("%.*f [%.*f, %.*f]", digits, x["Estimate"],
          digits, x["Q2.5"], digits, x["Q97.5"])
}
# Wall-clock of the slowest chain (chains run in parallel): the statistic the
# text reports as fitting time. Read from the archived fit, never typed.
fit_secs  <- function(fit) max(rowSums(rstan::get_elapsed_time(fit$fit)))
fit_time  <- function(fit) {
  s <- fit_secs(fit)
  if (s < 90) sprintf("%.0f s", s)
  else if (s < 3600) sprintf("%.1f min", s / 60)
  else sprintf("%.1f h", s / 3600)
}
# Bayes Factors: format (with infinity) and the verbal label the text uses
# (thresholds of 3, 10, 100 after @kass1995bayes, as introduced in Tutorial 1)
# Savage-Dickey ratios are density estimates from the posterior draws, and very
# large values are imprecise (Oberauer et al., 2026): anything at or above
# 10,000, including an underflow to infinity, prints as "$\geq$ 10,000". The
# helper returns the operator too, so prose writes "BF `r bf_fmt(x)`".
bf_fmt <- function(bf) {
  if (is.infinite(bf) || bf >= 1e4) return("$\\geq$ 10,000")
  paste("=", format(signif(bf, 2), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))
}
bf_label <- function(bf) {
  if (is.infinite(bf) || bf > 100) "decisive"
  else if (bf > 10) "strong"
  else if (bf > 3) "moderate"
  else "anecdotal"
}
# Drift rows of a fit as prose, for whatever stimulus factor the fit carries
.drift_labels <- c(high = "HF", low = "LF", very_low = "VLF", nonword = "NW", word = "word",
                   A = "stimulus A", B = "stimulus B")
.drift_rows <- function(fe) {
  rows <- grep("^drift_", rownames(fe), value = TRUE)
  lbl  <- sub("^drift_(stim_cat|freq|stimulus)", "", rows)
  lbl  <- ifelse(lbl %in% names(.drift_labels), .drift_labels[lbl], lbl)
  list(rows = rows, lbl = unname(lbl))
}
drift_txt <- function(fe, digits = 2) {
  d <- .drift_rows(fe)
  est <- apply(fe[d$rows, , drop = FALSE], 1, fmt_est, digits = digits)
  paste(sprintf("%s %s", d$lbl, est), collapse = "; ")
}
drift_order <- function(fe) {
  d <- .drift_rows(fe)
  paste(d$lbl[order(-fe[d$rows, "Estimate"])], collapse = " > ")
}
pending <- "[pending refit]"

# --- Fitted models, lexical decision data ------------------------------------
fit_acc_ezdm       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_acc_ezdm_freq  <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc_freq.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq.rds"))
fit_cswald_simple  <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple.rds"))
fit_cswald_resp    <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_ddm_acc        <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_ddm_resp       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp.rds"))

# --- Fitted models, simulated data (appendix recovery study) -----------------
fit_ezdm_3par    <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_3par.rds"))
fit_cswald_crisk <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_crisk.rds"))
fit_ddm          <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm.rds"))
true_params      <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
true_params_subject <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_subject.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)

# Cached prepared datasets, used to display the required data formats
data_accuracy_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_triallevel.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
data_acc_ezdm <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_ezdm3par.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
data_response_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_response_triallevel.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)

# --- Tutorial 1: EZ-Diffusion 3par (accuracy-coded) --------------------------
fe_t1 <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t1_ess  <- min(summary(fit_acc_ezdm)$fixed[, "Bulk_ESS"], na.rm = TRUE)
t1_time <- fit_time(fit_acc_ezdm)
# Divergent transitions across the eight lexical fits. The text states that
# none occurred, so the guard fails the render if a refit ever changes that.
.n_div <- function(fit) {
  np <- brms::nuts_params(fit)
  sum(np$Value[np$Parameter == "divergent__"])
}
n_div_all <- sum(sapply(list(fit_acc_ezdm, fit_resp_ezdm, fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
                             fit_resp_ezdm_freq, fit_cswald_simple, fit_cswald_resp,
                             fit_ddm_acc, fit_ddm_resp,
                             readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq_mix.rds"))),
                        .n_div))
stopifnot(n_div_all == 0)
t1_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catword", ])
t1_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t1_bound_speed   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_bound_acc     <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_ndt           <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# Equality hypotheses: Evid.Ratio is the Savage-Dickey BF *for* equality;
# its inverse quantifies the evidence against equality (reported as BF in text)
# Savage-Dickey evidence ratios vary slightly between hypothesis() calls, so
# each test is computed once with the seed argument; the printed output and
# the prose both read from that one object.
t1_hyp <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
), seed = 2026)
t1_bf_drift <- 1 / t1_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[1]
t1_bf_bound <- 1 / t1_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[2]

# --- Tutorial 1, frequency refit: EZ-Diffusion 3par with freq on drift -------
fe_t4f   <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t1f_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm_freq), na.rm = TRUE)
t1f_time <- fit_time(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t1f_hyp <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
                      c(high_vs_very_low = "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low"),
                      seed = 2026)
t1f_bf_drift <- 1 / t1f_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t1f_drift_order <- drift_order(fe_t4f)

# --- Tutorial 2: EZ-Diffusion 4par (response-coded) --------------------------
fe_t2 <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm)
t2_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t2_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catword", ])
t2_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t2_zr_speed <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_acc   <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_speed_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q97.5"]))
t2_zr_acc_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q97.5"]))
t2_hyp_drift_word <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword = 0", seed = 2026)
t2_bf_drift_word  <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_word$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_drift_nw   <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catnonword = 0", seed = 2026)
t2_bf_drift_nw    <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_nw$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t2_bf_bound  <- 1 / t2_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
# The starting point itself: zr = 0 on the logit scale is zeta_r = 0.5, an
# unbiased start. The inverse Evid.Ratio is the BF *against* an unbiased start
# (values below 1 favour it), which is what decides 3par vs 4par.
t2_hyp_zr <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, c(
  accuracy = "zr_conditionaccuracy = 0",
  speed    = "zr_conditionspeed = 0"
), seed = 2026)
t2_bf_zr_acc   <- 1 / t2_hyp_zr$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[1]
t2_bf_zr_speed <- 1 / t2_hyp_zr$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[2]
# Minority-boundary counts quoted under Trial-Count Constraint: "word" responses
# to nonwords under accuracy emphasis, per participant, in the data Tutorial 2 fits
.t2_minority <- data_response_clean |>
  dplyr::filter(stim_cat == "nonword", condition == "accuracy") |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_word = sum(response == "upper"), .by = id)
t2_minority_median <- median(.t2_minority$n_word)
t2_minority_min    <- min(.t2_minority$n_word)

# --- Part II: trial-level fits (cswald simple + crisk, ddm acc + resp) -------
fe_t3s <- fixef(fit_cswald_simple)
fe_t3c <- fixef(fit_cswald_resp)
fe_t4a <- fixef(fit_ddm_acc)
fe_t4r <- fixef(fit_ddm_resp)
t3_rhat_simple <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_simple), na.rm = TRUE)
t3_rhat_crisk  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_acc  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_acc), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_resp <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
# x2: cswald "simple" estimates bound on the single-boundary scale (see the
# Censored-Shifted Wald section), so double it to report the full separation.
t3s_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * 2)
t3s_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * 2)
t3s_ndt         <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# The simple version's drift has a log link (all other fits: identity), so its
# drift rows are back-transformed before they are printed or compared
fe_t3s_nat <- fe_t3s
.sd_rows <- grep("^drift_", rownames(fe_t3s_nat))
fe_t3s_nat[.sd_rows, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")] <- exp(fe_t3s[.sd_rows, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])
t3s_drift_txt   <- drift_txt(fe_t3s_nat)
t3c_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3c_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t3_bf_bound  <- 1 / t3_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_ndt         <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_drift_txt   <- drift_txt(fe_t4a)
t4_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t4_bf_bound  <- 1 / t4_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low", seed = 2026)
t4_bf_drift  <- 1 / t4_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
# Lower-boundary (error) counts in the response panel of the trial-level
# checks: observed, and the mean over the same 50 draws script 15 uses (same
# seed and the same order of fits, so the sampled draws are identical).
set.seed(1)
.pp_lower_counts <- function(fit) {
  d  <- sample(ndraws(fit), 50)
  pd <- pp_check(fit, resp_var = "response", draw_ids = d)$data
  k  <- which(pd$x == 0)
  # pd$m carries the quantile name "50%", which c() would append to "pred"
  c(obs = unname(pd$y_obs[k]), pred = round(unname(pd$m[k])))
}
t3s_pp_lower <- .pp_lower_counts(fit_cswald_simple)
t4a_pp_lower <- .pp_lower_counts(fit_ddm_acc)
stopifnot(t3s_pp_lower[["pred"]] < t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]],
          t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]] < t4a_pp_lower[["obs"]])

# --- Part III: EZ-Diffusion (freq) vs full DDM ---------------------------------
t4_ndt_ez  <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4f["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_ndt_ddm <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
.drift_lvls   <- c("freqhigh", "freqlow", "freqvery_low", "freqnonword")
.drift_ratios <- fe_t4f[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                 fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
t4_drift_pct_mean <- round((mean(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_lo   <- round((min(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_hi   <- round((max(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)

# Computational cost, read from the archived fits
.ezdm_secs <- purrr::map_dbl(list(fit_acc_ezdm, fit_resp_ezdm, fit_acc_ezdm_freq, fit_resp_ezdm_freq), fit_secs)
.fmt_secs  <- function(s) if (s < 90) sprintf("%.0f s", s) else if (s < 3600) sprintf("%.1f min", s / 60) else sprintf("%.1f h", s / 3600)
cost_ezdm_range     <- paste(.fmt_secs(min(.ezdm_secs)), "to", .fmt_secs(max(.ezdm_secs)))
cost_cswald_simple  <- fit_time(fit_cswald_simple)
cost_cswald_crisk   <- fit_time(fit_cswald_resp)
.ddm_secs <- purrr::map_dbl(list(fit_ddm_acc, fit_ddm_resp), fit_secs)
cost_ddm_range      <- paste(.fmt_secs(min(.ddm_secs)), "to", .fmt_secs(max(.ddm_secs)))
cost_factor         <- paste0("roughly ", format(signif(fit_secs(fit_ddm_acc) / fit_secs(fit_acc_ezdm_freq), 2), big.mark = ","))
cost_simple_share   <- round(100 * fit_secs(fit_cswald_simple) / fit_secs(fit_ddm_acc))
cost_crisk_share    <- round(100 * fit_secs(fit_cswald_resp) / fit_secs(fit_ddm_resp))

# --- Part III: orderings the prose states ---------------------------------------
# Each stopifnot() guards a sentence in the text: if a refit changes the ordering,
# the render fails instead of printing a claim the fits no longer support.
fe_t2f <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm_freq)
.bnd   <- function(fe, cond, m = 1) exp(fe[paste0("bound_condition", cond), "Estimate"]) * m
.pct   <- function(num, den) round((num / den - 1) * 100)
.conds <- c(accuracy = "accuracy", speed = "speed")
.ref_bound <- c(accuracy = 1.59, speed = 0.84)  # Wagenmakers et al. (2008), s = 1
bound_simple_excess <- sapply(.conds, \(c) .pct(.bnd(fe_t3s, c, 2), .bnd(fe_t4a, c)))
bound_ez_deficit    <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t4f, c), .bnd(fe_t4a, c)))
bound_ez4_deficit   <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t2f, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))
# The same 4par fit from mixture moments (script 15 section 1.3): how much of
# the gap to the full DDM is the robust-moment offset rather than the approach
fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq_mix.rds"))
fe_t2fm   <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix)
t2fm_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix), na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(t2fm_rhat < 1.01)
bound_ez4mix_deficit <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t2fm, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))
bound_ez4_offset_pts <- bound_ez4_deficit - bound_ez4mix_deficit
# The text says the mixture fit narrows the gap but does not close it
stopifnot(all(bound_ez4_offset_pts > 0), all(bound_ez4mix_deficit > 0))
mix_fallback <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_response_ezdm4par_freq_mix_fallback.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
bound_crisk_diff    <- max(abs(sapply(.conds, \(c) .pct(.bnd(fe_t3c, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))))
.ndt <- function(fe) exp(fe["ndt_Intercept", "Estimate"])
.simple_drift_ratio <- fe_t3s_nat[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                       fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
simple_drift_lo <- round((min(.simple_drift_ratio) - 1) * 100)
simple_drift_hi <- round((max(.simple_drift_ratio) - 1) * 100)
.word_order <- function(fe) all(diff(fe[paste0("drift_freq", c("high", "low", "very_low")), "Estimate"]) < 0)
stopifnot(
  # bound: EZ-Diffusion < full DDM < doubled simple cswald, in both conditions
  all(sapply(.conds, \(c) .bnd(fe_t4f, c) < .bnd(fe_t4a, c) && .bnd(fe_t4a, c) < .bnd(fe_t3s, c, 2))),
  bound_simple_excess["speed"] > bound_simple_excess["accuracy"],
  # EZ-Diffusion bound closest to the published values
  all(sapply(.conds, \(c) abs(.bnd(fe_t4f, c) - .ref_bound[c]) < abs(.bnd(fe_t4a, c) - .ref_bound[c]))),
  # ndt: EZ-Diffusion > full DDM > simple cswald
  .ndt(fe_t4f) > .ndt(fe_t4a), .ndt(fe_t4a) > .ndt(fe_t3s),
  # EZ-Diffusion drift at or above the full DDM's, most for high-frequency words
  min(.drift_ratios) > 0.99, which.max(.drift_ratios) == 1,
  # simple cswald drift above the full DDM's, furthest for very-low-frequency words
  all(.simple_drift_ratio > 1), which.max(.simple_drift_ratio) == 3,
  # word-frequency order of drift (high > low > very low) in all three approaches
  .word_order(fe_t4f), .word_order(fe_t3s), .word_order(fe_t4a),
  # bound higher under accuracy than speed emphasis in all five lexical fits
  all(sapply(list(fe_t4f, fe_t3s, fe_t4a, fe_t3c, fe_t4r, fe_t2f),
             \(fe) .bnd(fe, "accuracy") > .bnd(fe, "speed")))
)

# Cells that entered the 4par fits (robust moments are NA below min_trials)
lex_cells        <- nrow(dplyr::distinct(data_accuracy_clean, id, condition, stim_cat))
lex_cells_freq   <- nrow(dplyr::distinct(data_accuracy_clean, id, condition, freq))
t2_cells         <- nrow(fit_resp_ezdm$data)

# Cells with a boundary whose RT summaries are unusable: bmm keeps these
# and they enter through their response counts only. The indicator columns bmm
# adds to the data are 0 for such a boundary, so the count is read off the fit.
.counts_only <- function(fit)
  sum(fit$data$rt_used_upper == 0 | fit$data$rt_used_lower == 0)
t2_cells_counts_only <- .counts_only(fit_resp_ezdm)

# Posterior predictive checks of the two EZ-Diffusion fits: design cells whose
# observed statistic falls outside its 90% predictive interval, per observable.
# Same seed, draws, and order as scripts 11 and 12, so the counts match the figures.
.ppc_outside <- function(fit) {
  v <- pp_check_vars(fit)$resp_var
  set.seed(1)
  d <- sample(ndraws(fit), 50)
  sapply(v, \(r) {
    # type = "intervals" is required here: the default view for the ezdm RT
    # statistics is a density overlay, whose $data has no y_obs/ll/hh columns,
    # so the comparison below would silently count 0 cells for every statistic.
    pd <- suppressWarnings(
      pp_check(fit, resp_var = r, draw_ids = d, type = "intervals")
    )$data
    sum(pd$y_obs < pd$ll | pd$y_obs > pd$hh)
  })
}
t1_ppc_out  <- .ppc_outside(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1f_ppc_out <- .ppc_outside(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t2_ppc_out  <- .ppc_outside(fit_resp_ezdm)
# The same per-cell check for the four trial-level fits (script 15, section
# 2b, from the same 50 draws as their composite figure), read for the Part III
# table that puts all three approaches through one criterion
trial_ppc <- read_csv(here("data", "trial_level_ppc_cell_counts.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
.tp_count <- function(lbl, col) trial_ppc[[col]][trial_ppc$fit == lbl]
.tp_fits <- c(simple = "Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), accuracy-coded",
              ddm_acc = "Full DDM, accuracy-coded",
              crisk = "Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), response-coded",
              ddm_resp = "Full DDM, response-coded")
stopifnot(all(.tp_fits %in% trial_ppc$fit),
          all(trial_ppc$cells == lex_cells_freq))
# The text says the trial-level fits miss at least as many cells as the EZ
# refit and that RT variance is where each of them misses most
stopifnot(.tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "mean_rt") >= t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]],
          .tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "var_rt")  >= t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]],
          .tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "p_upper") >= t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]],
          all(trial_ppc$var_rt >= trial_ppc$mean_rt),
          all(trial_ppc$var_rt[trial_ppc$fit != .tp_fits[["simple"]]] >=
              trial_ppc$p_upper[trial_ppc$fit != .tp_fits[["simple"]]]))
ppc_cells_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Fit = c("EZ-Diffusion Model (3par, frequency refit)", "Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)",
          "Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk)", "Full DDM, response-coded"),
  `Mean RT`     = c(t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "mean_rt")),
  `RT variance` = c(t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "var_rt")),
  `Proportion upper` = c(t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "p_upper"))
)

# Lexical-data facts quoted in Part II and III: accuracy-coded error rates by
# emphasis x frequency cell, and the fastest RT left after cleaning
.err <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  dplyr::summarise(err = 100 * mean(response == "lower"), .by = c(condition, freq)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(err)
.ne <- nrow(.err)
err_min    <- sprintf("%.1f", .err$err[1])
err_second <- sprintf("%.1f", .err$err[.ne - 1])
err_max    <- sprintf("%.1f", .err$err[.ne])
stopifnot(.err$condition[1] == "accuracy", .err$freq[1] == "high",
          .err$condition[.ne - 1] == "speed", .err$freq[.ne - 1] == "low",
          .err$condition[.ne] == "speed", .err$freq[.ne] == "very_low",
          .err$err[.ne - 1] < 20, .err$err[.ne] > 20)
min_rt_ms <- round(1000 * min(data_accuracy_clean$rt))
ez4f_cells       <- nrow(fit_resp_ezdm_freq$data)
ez4f_cells_counts_only <- .counts_only(fit_resp_ezdm_freq)
stopifnot(t2_cells_counts_only > 0, t2_cells_counts_only < t2_cells,
          ez4f_cells_counts_only > 0, ez4f_cells_counts_only < ez4f_cells)

# --- Part I: recovery with a biased starting point (scripts/22) ----------------
# Guarded: every quantity is a placeholder until the three fits exist.
.bias_vars <- c("bias_trials_per_cell", "bias_zr_A", "bias_zr_B", "bias_ddm_zr_A", "bias_ddm_zr_B",
                "bias_drift_4par", "bias_drift_3par", "bias_drift_ddm", "bias_drift_true",
                "bias_bound_4par", "bias_bound_3par", "bias_bound_ddm",
                "bias_r_zr_min", "bias_r_zr_max", "bias_time_4par", "bias_time_3par", "bias_time_ddm",
                "bias_bound_rhat_max", "bias_bound_ess_min")
for (.v in .bias_vars) assign(.v, pending)
.bias_fits <- here("output", c("fit_ezdm_4par_bias.rds", "fit_ezdm_3par_bias.rds", "fit_ddm_bias.rds"))
bias_ok <- all(file.exists(.bias_fits)) &&
  file.exists(here("data", "true_parameters_bias.csv")) &&
  file.exists(here("data", "true_parameters_bias_subject.csv")) &&
  file.exists(here("figures", "22_bias_recovery_group.pdf"))
if (bias_ok) {
  fit_ezdm_4par_bias <- readRDS(.bias_fits[1])
  fit_ezdm_3par_bias <- readRDS(.bias_fits[2])
  fit_ddm_bias       <- readRDS(.bias_fits[3])
  true_bias <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_bias.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  true_bias_subject <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_bias_subject.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  bias_trials_per_cell <- unique(true_bias$n_trials_cell)
  bias_drift_true <- sprintf("%.1f", abs(true_bias$drift[1]))
  fe_b4 <- fixef(fit_ezdm_4par_bias); fe_b3 <- fixef(fit_ezdm_3par_bias); fe_bd <- fixef(fit_ddm_bias)
  .zr <- function(fe, row) fmt_est(plogis(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
  bias_zr_A <- .zr(fe_b4, "zr_biasA"); bias_zr_B <- .zr(fe_b4, "zr_biasB")
  bias_ddm_zr_A <- .zr(fe_bd, "zr_biasA"); bias_ddm_zr_B <- .zr(fe_bd, "zr_biasB")
  bias_drift_4par <- drift_txt(fe_b4); bias_drift_3par <- drift_txt(fe_b3); bias_drift_ddm <- drift_txt(fe_bd)
  .bd <- function(fe) fmt_est(exp(fe["bound_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
  bias_bound_4par <- .bd(fe_b4); bias_bound_3par <- .bd(fe_b3); bias_bound_ddm <- .bd(fe_bd)
  bias_cors <- read_csv(here("data", "bias_recovery_subject_correlations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  # Only zr is interpreted (bound did not converge), so only its correlations are quoted
  .zr_cors <- bias_cors$r[startsWith(bias_cors$parameter, "zr")]
  bias_r_zr_min <- sprintf("%.2f", min(.zr_cors)); bias_r_zr_max <- sprintf("%.2f", max(.zr_cors))
  bias_time_4par <- fit_time(fit_ezdm_4par_bias); bias_time_3par <- fit_time(fit_ezdm_3par_bias)
  bias_time_ddm  <- fit_time(fit_ddm_bias)
  # Convergence of the population-level bound, the parameter all three fits mix slowly on
  .bias_bound_diag <- sapply(list(fit_ezdm_4par_bias, fit_ezdm_3par_bias, fit_ddm_bias), \(f) {
    d <- posterior::summarise_draws(
      posterior::subset_draws(posterior::as_draws_array(f), variable = "b_bound_Intercept"),
      "rhat", "ess_bulk")
    c(d$rhat, d$ess_bulk)
  })
  bias_bound_rhat_max <- sprintf("%.3f", max(.bias_bound_diag[1, ]))
  bias_bound_ess_min  <- round(min(.bias_bound_diag[2, ]))
}

# Appendix: Subject-level recovery correlations
extract_subject_params <- function(fit, model_name, n_subjects = 50) {
  co <- coef(fit)$id
  bind_rows(
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_easy",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditioneasy"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_hard",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditionhard"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "bound",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "bound_Intercept"])),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "ndt",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "ndt_Intercept"]))
  )
}

subject_recovery <- bind_rows(
  extract_subject_params(fit_ezdm_3par, "EZ-Diffusion 3par"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_cswald_crisk, "Censored-Shifted Wald crisk"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_ddm, "DDM")
)

true_subject <- bind_rows(
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_easy", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "hard") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_hard", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "bound", true_value = bound_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "ndt", true_value = ndt_subj)
)

subject_recovery <- subject_recovery |>
  left_join(true_subject, by = c("id", "parameter"))

recovery_cors <- subject_recovery |>
  group_by(model, parameter) |>
  summarise(r = cor(true_value, recovered), .groups = "drop")

recovery_r_min <- round(min(recovery_cors$r), 2)
recovery_r_max <- round(max(recovery_cors$r), 2)
# Correlations by approach and parameter, for the appendix table, and the
# lowest one for the prose
.rec_model_lbl <- c("EZ-Diffusion 3par" = "EZ-Diffusion Model (3par)",
                    "Censored-Shifted Wald crisk" = "Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk)",
                    "DDM" = "Full DDM")
.rec_param_lbl <- c(drift_easy = "Drift (easy)", drift_hard = "Drift (hard)",
                    bound = "Bound", ndt = "ndt")
recovery_cors_lbl <- recovery_cors |>
  mutate(model = .rec_model_lbl[model], parameter = .rec_param_lbl[parameter])
recovery_cors_tab <- recovery_cors_lbl |>
  mutate(r = sprintf("%.2f", r)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = parameter, values_from = r) |>
  rename(Approach = model)
.rmin <- recovery_cors_lbl[which.min(recovery_cors_lbl$r), ]
recovery_r_min_model <- .rmin$model
recovery_r_min_param <- .rmin$parameter
stopifnot(all(recovery_cors$r >= 0.70))

# Appendix: group-level coverage of the generating values. Each stopifnot()
# line guards a sentence in the appendix text.
.tp  <- true_params[1, ]  # bound, ndt, and zr are constant across conditions
.gl  <- function(fit, row, f = identity) {
  x <- fixef(fit)[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]
  setNames(f(x), names(x))
}
.covers <- function(v, x) v >= x[["Q2.5"]] && v <= x[["Q97.5"]]
.rec_fits <- list(fit_ezdm_3par, fit_cswald_crisk, fit_ddm)
.drift_true <- setNames(true_params$drift, true_params$condition)
rec_ndt_ez  <- fmt_est(.gl(fit_ezdm_3par, "ndt_Intercept", exp), 3)
rec_ndt_ddm <- fmt_est(.gl(fit_ddm, "ndt_Intercept", exp), 3)
rec_crisk_bound     <- fmt_est(.gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "bound_Intercept", exp))
rec_crisk_bound_pct <- round((1 - .gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "bound_Intercept", exp)[["Estimate"]] / .tp$bound) * 100)
rec_crisk_zr        <- fmt_est(.gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "zr_Intercept", plogis), 3)
stopifnot(
  all(sapply(.rec_fits, \(f) .covers(.drift_true[["easy"]], .gl(f, "drift_conditioneasy")) &&
                              .covers(.drift_true[["hard"]], .gl(f, "drift_conditionhard")))),
  .covers(.tp$bound, .gl(fit_ezdm_3par, "bound_Intercept", exp)),
  .covers(.tp$bound, .gl(fit_ddm, "bound_Intercept", exp)),
  !.covers(.tp$bound, .gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "bound_Intercept", exp)),
  .covers(.tp$ndt, .gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "ndt_Intercept", exp)),
  !.covers(.tp$ndt, .gl(fit_ezdm_3par, "ndt_Intercept", exp)),
  !.covers(.tp$ndt, .gl(fit_ddm, "ndt_Intercept", exp)),
  !.covers(.tp$zr, .gl(fit_cswald_crisk, "zr_Intercept", plogis))
)
recovery_r_median <- round(median(recovery_cors$r), 2)
```


# Introduction

Consider two participants performing a speeded choice task, for example deciding if a digit is odd or even. Participant A has an average response time of correct responses of 550 ms and an accuracy of 90%; Participant B has an average response time of correct responses of 600 ms with an accuracy of 95%. Who would you say performed better on the task? An analysis focussing on reaction times would favor participant A while an analysis focussing on accuracy would favor B. However, neither of the summary statistics alone can provide evidence *why* and *how* these participants differ in the underlying cognitive processes. In our example, participant A may extract evidence faster but set a more liberal decision threshold, while participant B may extract evidence at the same rate but set a more cautious response threshold that trades speed for accuracy. Traditional analyses focussing on mean RT and accuracy separately are insufficient for such inferences; they confound effects of different underlying processes and are not process pure measures of the underlying cognitive processes [@frischkorn2026validity].

The by now ubiquitous way to address this issue is to use mathematical models that describe how the underlying latent cognitive processes give rise to the observed behavioral performance. Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) jointly model response times (RTs) and responses or accuracy from speeded decision-making tasks to decompose observed performance into latent cognitive parameters: the rate of evidence accumulation, the amount of evidence required before responding, and the time consumed by non-decisional processes such as stimulus encoding and motor execution. Since their introduction [@ratcliff1978theory], EAMs have become the standard framework for analyzing RT data across perception, memory retrieval, and cognitive control [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @donkin2018response; @evans2019evidence].

The Diffusion Decision Model [DDM; @ratcliff1978theory] is the most widely applied EAM for two-choice tasks. By now it is supported by decades of empirical validation across cognitive domains [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The DDM is one member of a broader family of accumulation architectures; alternatives include race models such as the Linear Ballistic Accumulator and competitive models in which accumulators inhibit each other [@brown2008lba; @rouder2015lnr; @tillman2020racing; @usher2001lca]. These are beyond the scope of this tutorial, and it will focus only on the DDM [for reviews, see @ratcliff2004comparison; @forstmann2016review; @boag2025expert].

Within the DDM framework, multiple estimation approaches have been proposed that differ in data requirements, computational cost, and their underlying assumptions [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @anders2016shifted; @ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. All of them estimate the same core DDM parameters, drift, boundary separation, non-decision time, and (optionally) relative starting point, but extract these parameters from data at different levels of granularity: from aggregated summary statistics, or from trial-level RT distributions either using distributional approximations or the mathematically accurate Wiener first-passage time likelihood. Choosing among these approaches involves balancing trade-offs that are complicated by the fact that RT data oftentimes contain contaminant responses, such as premature responses, or attentional lapses. These bias parameter estimates [@ratcliff2002estimating; @ratcliff2008ez; @boag2025expert] and affect different estimation procedures to varying degrees. 

Although many software options for estimating DDM parameters have been developed over the recent years, each of the above mentioned approaches required its own specialized software, making cross-approach comparison difficult. The `bmm` R package [@frischkorn2025tutorial] now addresses this by implementing three DDM estimation approaches, the EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the Censored-Shifted Wald [`cswald`; @anders2016shifted] as a distributional proxy, and full DDM likelihood estimation [`ddm`]. All three approaches are implemented in a unified Bayesian hierarchical framework built on `brms` [@burkner2017brms] and Stan [@cmdstanr2024]. The consistent interface means that switching between estimation approaches requires changing only the model object, while the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools remain identical.[^future]

[^future]: The implementation of race-model architectures in `bmm` may follow in future versions of the package.

Estimating DDM parameters within a Bayesian hierarchical framework offers several advantages over the single-subject maximum likelihood approaches that dominated earlier work. Hierarchical estimation borrows information across participants, producing more stable individual-level estimates even with moderate trial counts [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical], a common practical constraint in multi-condition designs. It propagates uncertainty through posterior distributions rather than point estimates, and it handles the unbalanced cell sizes that arise when some conditions produce few errors [@boehm2018shortcuts]. For the EZ-Diffusion Model the consequences are the largest. Originally a calculator that turns three summary statistics into three parameters, it becomes, once recast as a likelihood [@chavez2025ez], a full hierarchical model that accepts predictors on any parameter, and it keeps its speed: the fits in this tutorial take seconds to minutes where the full DDM takes hours. This is the central message of the tutorial. For the questions applied work most often asks, whether a manipulation changes drift, boundary separation, or the starting point, and whether individuals differ, the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model reaches the same conclusions as the full DDM, on a time scale that makes iterating on a model specification routine rather than costly.

This tutorial is written for researchers with basic familiarity with R and hierarchical Bayesian regression models estimated via `brms` who have collected or plan to collect two-choice RT data. After completing it, you will be able to:

1. Preprocess RT data to detect and handle contaminant responses with `bmm`'s dedicated functions.
2. Specify, fit, and evaluate the EZ-Diffusion Model as a primary analysis of condition effects on drift, boundary separation, and non-decision time; extend it to response bias with the four-parameter version; and judge when the starting point has to be estimated rather than fixed.
3. Fit the trial-level approaches, the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM, at the same specification.
4. Decide which approach your research question needs, and read the differences between them.

The tutorial is organized in three parts. Part I introduces the EZ-Diffusion Model on the by now classical lexical decision data [@wagenmakers2008lexical] and adds a parameter recovery study with a biased starting point. Part II fits the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM at the specification Part I arrived at. Part III compares the three approaches and turns the comparison into practical guidelines.

The tutorial focuses on the simple (four-parameter) DDM framework for two-choice tasks. It does not cover the full DDM with between-trial variability parameters, race-model architectures (e.g., the LBA or racing diffusion model), multi-alternative choice tasks, or formal model comparison techniques such as leave-one-out cross-validation or bridge sampling; these are available via `brms` but beyond the scope of this tutorial.

# Background: Evidence Accumulation Models

## The Diffusion Model Framework

To build intuition for what the DDM captures, consider the following example. In a lexical decision task, a participant sees the letter string "CHAIR" on screen and is instructed to press one of two buttons to indicate if the target stimulus is a "word" or "nonword." Upon stimulus onset, the participant begins extracting evidence such as orthographic regularity, phonological plausibility, or lexical familiarity that accumulates noisily over time toward one of two response boundaries. If the accumulated evidence reaches the "word" boundary first, the participant responds "word"; if it instead reaches the "nonword" boundary, they respond "nonword". The observed RT is the sum of this decision time and non-decisional components such as stimulus encoding and motor execution. See @fig-diffusion-schematic for an illustration of this process.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffusion-schematic
#| fig-cap: "Schematic of the Diffusion Decision Model"
#| apa-note: "Evidence accumulates noisily from the starting point ($\\zeta_r$) toward one of two response boundaries separated by distance $\\alpha$, with the mean rate of accumulation given by the drift ($\\delta$). Accumulation begins only once the stimulus has been encoded (shaded region) and the response is registered only after motor execution (dashed segments): the non-decision time $\\tau$ is the sum of these two intervals. Because the model estimates only that sum, the split drawn here is illustrative. Several example paths are shown (blue: reaching the upper boundary, correct response; red: reaching the lower boundary, error). The distributions attached to each boundary show the resulting response times, right-skewed for correct responses and errors alike (the error distribution's height is exaggerated for visibility)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "03_diffusion_schematic.pdf"))
```

This example illustrates the core assumptions of the DDM [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion], and it also shows the four parameters that each capture a distinct aspect of the decision process:

- Drift Rate ($\delta$ or `drift`): The mean rate of evidence accumulation, reflecting stimulus quality or strength. Higher drift yields faster and more accurate responses.
- Boundary separation ($\alpha$ or `bound`): The distance between the two response boundaries, capturing *response caution*. Wider boundaries require more evidence, yielding slower but more accurate responses.
- Non-decision time ($\tau$ or `ndt`): The portion of the observed RT not attributable to the decision process, encompassing *stimulus encoding*, which precedes evidence accumulation, and *motor execution*, which follows it. Only the sum of the two is estimated; the model does not separate them.
- Relative starting point ($\zeta_r$ or `zr`): The starting point of evidence accumulation between the two boundaries, expressed as a proportion relative to the boundary separation (0.5 = unbiased). Values deviating from 0.5 indicate an *a priori response bias* towards the upper or lower response.

One additional parameter, the diffusion noise $s$ that captures the standard deviation of the noise during evidence accumulation, is usually fixed to 1 to set the scale of the other parameters. Freely estimating the diffusion constant together with the other DDM parameters under-identifies the parameters space [@nunez2025identifiable]. In principle, bmm offers the option to estimate $s$ as well, but without additional external data to set the scale of the evidence accumulation this requires that either drift or boundary separation are fixed for model identification. In this tutorial we will not estimate $s$ and instead fix it to 1, which is the standard approach in the literature.

Each of these parameters is meant to correspond to a distinct cognitive process. Thus, the DDM makes testable predictions about how experimental manipulations should affect behavior if they target a specific process. This principle of *selective influence* has been demonstrated with stimulus quality manipulations (e.g., degradation, word frequency) that affect drift but not boundary separation or non-decision time, and with *response caution* manipulations (e.g., speed–accuracy instructions) that uniquely affect boundary separation [@voss2004interpreting; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. This evidence for selective influence is a central part of the validity of the DDM [see @boag2025expert, Table 2, for a comprehensive overview].

The four-parameter formulation described above is sometimes called the *simple* or *pure* DDM. The *full* DDM [@ratcliff2002estimating] adds three trial-to-trial variability parameters: variability in drift (trials with low trial-to-trial drift end slowly and often at the wrong boundary, producing slow errors), variability in the starting point (trials starting near the wrong boundary reach it quickly, producing fast errors), and variability in ndt (to account for leading-edge variation in RT distributions). These additions increase the model's flexibility, but also its complexity and computational cost, and the added parameters are often difficult to recover reliably from data [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @boehm2018variability]. For many applications — especially when the goal is to detect condition effects on drift or bound rather than to characterize the precise shape of error RT distributions — the simple DDM is the more parsimonious and statistically powerful choice [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Moreover, the computational cost of estimating trial-to-trial variability parameters in Bayesian hierarchical modeling is high and likely infeasible for larger individual differences studies or experimental designs with several experimental factors.[^feasibility] Therefore, all three estimation approaches in `bmm` are based on the simple DDM framework.

[^feasibility]: In the collaborative estimation exercise reported by @boehm2018variability, a hierarchical data set of 20 simulated participants with a single difficulty manipulation already sat at the edge of what was feasible for expert teams, with one hierarchical fit taking about 14 hours on four cores, another team able to run only a single MCMC chain in the time available, and a third abandoning hierarchical estimation altogether. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks shifts this cost into a one-time training phase and has been used to estimate the variability parameters in samples of several million participants [@vonkrause2026scaling]. For now, however, this means returning to two-step inference: parameters are estimated per participant and only then related to predictors.

## DDM Estimation Approaches in bmm

The `bmm` package implements three approaches for estimating DDM parameters that share the same theoretical framework but differ in data requirements and computational cost. @tbl-model-comparison summarizes the key differences; the distributions named in its Likelihood row are unpacked in the subsections that follow.

| Feature | EZ-Diffusion Model | Censored-Shifted Wald | Full DDM |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `bmm` function | `ezdm()` | `cswald()` | `ddm()` |
| Data required | Aggregated per cell: mean RT, RT variance, accuracy | Trial-level: RT, response | Trial-level: RT, response |
| Likelihood | Closed-form EZ equations | Shifted Wald, errors censored (simple) or racing accumulators (crisk) | Wiener first-passage time |
| Min trials/cell | ~30 (3par); ~30 per boundary (4par) | ~50 | ~50 |
| Fitting time | `r cost_ezdm_range` | `r cost_cswald_simple` (simple), `r cost_cswald_crisk` (crisk) | `r cost_ddm_range` |
| Best suited for | Primary analysis of condition effects and individual differences; exploration across many conditions | Trial-level analysis of high-accuracy data (< ~20% errors), including iterative model development (simple); response bias when errors are frequent (crisk) | Confirmatory analysis; RT-distribution shape; absolute values of bound and ndt |

: Summary of the three DDM Estimation Approaches in `bmm` {#tbl-model-comparison apa-note="Parameter symbols used throughout: drift $\delta$, boundary separation (bound) $\alpha$, non-decision time (ndt) $\tau$, relative starting point $\zeta_r$. Fitting times are wall-clock times of the slowest chain on the lexical decision data (Part III), measured on an Apple M3 Max with five chains, two threads per chain, and one fit at a time."}

### EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion] was developed to make diffusion model analysis quick and easy by eliminating the need for iterative fitting routines. Its starting point is that for a diffusion process with an unbiased starting point, three quantities — the probability of reaching the upper boundary, the mean decision time, and the variance of the decision time — have closed-form expressions in terms of drift and bound alone. Writing $\delta$ for drift, $\alpha$ for bound, and setting the diffusion noise $s = 1$, with $y = -\alpha\delta$:

$$
P(\text{upper}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{MDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta} \cdot \frac{1 - e^{y}}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{VDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta^{3}} \cdot \frac{2y e^{y} - e^{2y} + 1}{(1 + e^{y})^{2}}
$$

where MDT and VDT are the mean and variance of the decision time, and $n$ below is the number of trials in the cell (`n_trials`). The observed mean RT is MDT plus ndt; the observed RT variance is VDT, since a constant ndt shifts the distribution without spreading it. The original formulation inverted these expressions to compute parameter estimates directly from the observed summary statistics, which is what made EZ-Diffusion analysis a calculator exercise rather than a fitting problem.

The rest of this subsection sets out the likelihood `bmm` builds from these equations; nothing in it is needed to run the first fit, so a reader who wants to fit first can continue with the Lexical Decision Dataset and return here from Part I. `bmm` runs these equations in the forward direction instead, following the probabilistic reformulation of @chavez2025ez. Instead of the inversion, it treats the three summary statistics of each cell as noisy observations of the values the model predicts for them and gives them a joint sampling distribution. The response count is binomial. The two RT summaries follow the sampling distribution of the mean and the variance of $n$ decision times, which depends on the first four cumulants of the decision-time distribution (cumulants are the moment-like quantities that add over independent components; the first two are the mean and the variance): its mean MDT, its variance VDT, and its third and fourth cumulants $\kappa_3$ and $\kappa_4$, which carry the skew and the tail weight. These cumulants are not computed from the observed RTs. They are the values the DDM implies for the current drift, bound, and zr, recomputed whenever the parameters change. For an unbiased starting point, MDT and VDT are the expressions above; @grasman2009ez give them for any starting point, separately for each boundary. @srivastava2016moments [Eq. 28, p. 101] derived the cumulant generating function of the decision time conditional on the response and from it the first three moments. `bmm` obtains $\kappa_3$ and $\kappa_4$ by differentiating that function three and four times, an extension @srivastava2016moments [p. 105] note is possible but do not carry out (see `?ezdm_dist`). The likelihood is then

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{\text{upper}} &\sim \text{Binomial}\big(n, P(\text{upper})\big), \\
s^{2}_{\text{RT}} &\sim \text{Gamma}\!\left(\tfrac{\text{VDT}^{2}}{W},\; \tfrac{\text{VDT}}{W}\right), \\
\overline{\text{RT}} \mid s^{2}_{\text{RT}} &\sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\tau + \text{MDT} + \tfrac{\kappa_3 / n}{W}\,\big(s^{2}_{\text{RT}} - \text{VDT}\big),\; \sqrt{\tfrac{\text{VDT}}{n} - \tfrac{(\kappa_3 / n)^{2}}{W}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
W = \frac{\kappa_4}{n} + \frac{2\,\text{VDT}^{2}}{n - 1}
$$

is the variance of the sample variance. In words: the sample variance is Gamma-distributed around VDT with a spread that the fourth cumulant widens, and the sample mean is Normal around $\tau + \text{MDT}$, shifted by however far the observed variance sits from its expectation, because in a right-skewed distribution the two statistics are correlated. When $\kappa_3 = \kappa_4 = 0$ this reduces to independent Normal and scaled chi-square terms, the form that treats RTs as if they were normally distributed, which was proposed by @chavez2025ez.

Specifying the model this way makes hierarchical estimation with arbitrary regression structures on the parameters possible: there is now a likelihood to which priors, random effects, and predictors can be attached. It also makes the dependence on preprocessing explicit. The data entering this likelihood are $n_{\text{upper}}$, $\overline{\text{RT}}$, and $s^{2}_{\text{RT}}$ so anything that distorts those summary statistics distorts the parameter estimates.

The speed comes at the cost of two limitations: no trial-to-trial variability in any parameter can be estimated, and an unbiased starting point ($\zeta_r = 0.5$) is assumed. When these are violated, estimates can be biased. Nevertheless, the model remains a powerful tool for detecting condition effects, with prior simulation work reporting statistical power comparable to or higher than the full DDM [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions].

The `bmm` package includes two extensions of the EZ-Diffusion Model. *Robust-EZ* fits a two-component mixture — a uniform distribution for contaminant RTs and an ex-Gaussian (an exponentially modified Gaussian, the standard descriptive RT distribution) for the decision process — and feeds the ex-Gaussian component's mean and variance, rather than the raw sample moments, into the EZ equations [@wagenmakers2008extensions]; this is implemented in the mixture method of `ezdm_summary_stats()` introduced in the Data Preprocessing section. Moreover, a four-parameter extension estimates the relative starting point from separately computed mean and variance of RTs for upper and lower boundary responses [@grasman2009ez; @srivastava2016moments]; this is shown in Tutorial 2.

### Censored-Shifted Wald Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model's speed comes from working with summary statistics, but this means it cannot incorporate trial-level predictors or preserve information about the shape of the RT distribution. The full DDM preserves all of this but is computationally expensive. The Censored-Shifted Wald [`cswald` in `bmm`; @anders2016shifted] offers an intermediate path: it models individual RTs directly, preserving distributional information and enabling trial-level predictors, while remaining faster than the full DDM.

The Censored-Shifted Wald model achieves this by using the shifted Wald (inverse Gaussian) distribution. The shifted Wald distribution describes the *first-passage time* — the moment an accumulation path like those in @fig-diffusion-schematic first touches a boundary — for a diffusion process with a single *absorbing* boundary, meaning a boundary at which the process stops as soon as it arrives [@anders2016shifted]. This is a simpler process than the two-boundary framework of the DDM, and therefore faster to evaluate. Crucially, when error rates are low — because drift is high, bound is wide, or responses are biased toward the correct boundary — the shifted Wald parameters closely approximate those of the distribution that underlies the full DDM [@miller2018shifted]. In other words, when most responses are correct, the decision process behaves as if there were effectively only one boundary to reach, and the Censored-Shifted Wald captures this well.

The `bmm` package implements two versions proposed by @miller2018shifted that handle error responses differently. The *simple* version treats an error as a *censored* correct response. The model thus describes how long it takes to reach the correct boundary, while on an error trial it is assumed the correct boundary was never reached. What the trial tells us is not a completion time but a lower bound — however long the correct-boundary process would eventually have taken, it was longer than the RT we observed, because at that moment the participant responded and we stopped observing. This translates into the likelihood that is composed of two components: A correct response at time $t$ contributes the shifted Wald density $f$, while an error at time $t$ contributes the *survival function* $S(t) = 1 - F(t)$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function of $f$. The survival function is simply the probability that the correct-boundary process had not finished by $t$:

$$
\mathcal{L}(t) =
\begin{cases}
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) & \text{correct response} \\[4pt]
S(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = 1 - \displaystyle\int_{\tau}^{t} f(u \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau)\, du & \text{error}
\end{cases}
$$

with the shifted Wald density itself given by

$$
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = \frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{2\pi (t - \tau)^{3}}} \, \exp\!\left(-\frac{\big(\alpha - \delta (t-\tau)\big)^{2}}{2 (t - \tau)}\right), \qquad t > \tau
$$

again with the diffusion constant being fixed for scaling $s = 1$. Note that here $\alpha$ denotes the distance from the starting point to the single absorbing boundary, not the separation between two boundaries. For an unbiased starting point the two differ by a factor of 2, and `bmm` reports the simple version's bound on this single-boundary scale, so its estimates must be doubled before they are compared with those of `ezdm`, `ddm`, or the competing-risks version described next.

Although the cswald model assumes only a single bound for correct or upper responses, error trials are still *used*, not discarded. They enter the likelihood through the survival function. But a censored trial only bounds the completion time from below, so it constrains the parameters less tightly than a correct response does, and the approximation degrades as errors become more frequent. This is the reason why the cswald model should only be used with less than 20% lower bound or error responses [@miller2018shifted].

To accommodate for biases at larger rates of lower bound or error responses, the *competing-risks* (crisk) version models both correct and error RTs explicitly, as two independent racing shifted Wald processes that share the same non-decision time. The first shifted Wald accumulator to finish produces the observed response. This also enables the estimation of the relative starting point. Thus, at higher error rates, or when response bias is of interest for the research question, the competing-risks version provides a better approximation to the Wiener distribution [@miller2018shifted].

### The DDM Model

The DDM model [`ddm` in `bmm`] uses the Wiener first-passage time distribution to jointly model both the RT and the response boundary that was reached [@ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. Unlike the Censored-Shifted Wald, which approximates the decision process with one or two independent single-boundary accumulators, the full DDM implements the two-boundary process directly. This means it simultaneously captures the probability of reaching each boundary *and* the complete distribution of times to reach it, making it the mathematically accurate and complete characterization of the evidence accumulation process described above. The price is that this density has no closed form: the first-passage density at the upper boundary is an infinite series in $\alpha$, $\delta$, $\zeta_r$, and $t - \tau$ [@navarro2009fast], and the lower-boundary density is obtained by replacing $\delta$ with $-\delta$ and $\zeta_r$ with $1-\zeta_r$, which is exactly what `bmm` does.[^absolute-z] The infinite sum is the source of the computational cost: every likelihood evaluation must truncate the series, and how many terms that takes depends on the reaction time $t$, so implementations switch adaptively between this expansion and a complementary small-time one [@navarro2009fast]. Likelihood computation is therefore substantially more expensive than for the `ezdm` or `cswald` approaches. Various estimation methods such as chi-square fitting [@ratcliff2002estimating], maximum likelihood [@vandekerckhove2007fitting; @voss2007fastdm], and hierarchical Bayesian methods [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical; @wiecki2013hddm] have been developed over the years. In `bmm`, the full DDM is fitted via Stan's `wiener_lpdf()` function, which implements efficient series truncation within a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework.

[^absolute-z]: Much of the literature states this substitution on the absolute starting-point scale: writing $z = \alpha\zeta_r$ for the absolute starting point, the lower-boundary density follows by replacing $\delta$ with $-\delta$ and $z$ with $\alpha - z$. The two are the same substitution, since $(\alpha - z)/\alpha = 1 - \zeta_r$. We use the relative form throughout because $\zeta_r$ is what `bmm` estimates and reports.

## Estimating DDM Parameters with Existing Software

Each of the different models has been implemented in established software, with most packages historically focussing on a single estimation approach: `fast-dm` for $\chi^2$ and maximum-likelihood fitting of the full DDM [@voss2007fastdm], HDDM for hierarchical Bayesian DDM estimation in Python [@wiecki2013hddm], `rtdists` for DDM and LBA densities in R [@singmann2016rtdists], and spreadsheet or script implementations of the EZ-Diffusion equations [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. The exception is the R package `EMC2` [@stevenson2026emc2], which, like `bmm`, provides a general hierarchical Bayesian framework for evidence accumulation models, and which is the closest point of comparison. @tbl-software summarizes how the different software packages relate to `bmm`.[^development]

[^development]: Both `EMC2` and `bmm` are comparatively new packages under active development. The range of models each covers, and the features compared in @tbl-software, are those available at the time of writing; both can be expected to grow.

| Feature | `fast-dm`, `rtdists` | Standalone EZ-Diffusion | HDDM | `EMC2` | `bmm` |
|:--------------|:---------------|:---------------|:--------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| Estimation | Maximum likelihood or $\chi^2$ | Closed-form calculation | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian |
| Sampler | Numerical optimization | None | Slice sampling (PyMC) | Particle Metropolis-within-Gibbs | Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan) |
| Uncertainty | Point estimates (+ bootstrap) | Point estimates | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions |
| Multiple conditions | Fit separately per condition | Computed separately per cell | Regression syntax | Formula per parameter (`design()`) | Formula per parameter (`bmf()`) |
| Inference over conditions | Stepwise | Stepwise | One step | One step | One step |
| Continuous predictors | No | No | Limited | Yes | Yes |
| Predictors per parameter | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Grouping factors | None | None | Participants | Participants | Any `brms` structure (participants, items, crossed) |
| Parameter covariance | No | No | No | Full, blocked, diagonal, or factor-analytic | Optional, via linked terms |
| Trials per cell | Several hundred | ~30 | ~50 | ~50 | ~30 (`ezdm`) to ~50 (trial-level) |
| Models covered | Full DDM | EZ-Diffusion | Full DDM | Full DDM, LBA, RDM, LNR, custom likelihoods | Three DDM approaches, one interface |
| Post-processing | Package-specific | Manual | Package-specific | Package-specific | The `brms` ecosystem |

: Comparison of `bmm` With Existing Software for Estimating DDM Parameters {#tbl-software apa-note="`fast-dm` and `rtdists` fit each participant separately by maximum likelihood (ML). Stepwise: effects tested on point estimates, ignoring their uncertainty [@boehm2018shortcuts]. Sampler of `EMC2`: @gunawan2020pmwg. Four-parameter `ezdm`: ~30 trials per boundary."}

With respect to the benefits of `EMC2` and `bmm` over each other, `EMC2` covers far more of the evidence accumulation family: the full DDM including its across-trial variability parameters, the linear ballistic accumulator, racing diffusion and lognormal race models, and also allows user to specify their own models with user-supplied likelihoods. It also treats the group level as a modeling target in its own right, estimating a covariance matrix across participants' parameters. `bmm` currently implements only the DDM, and only in its simple form, partly because Stan requires a differentiable likelihood. If your question concerns a race architecture, the across-trial variability parameters, or how parameters covary across people, `EMC2` is the better tool.

The benefit of `bmm` is its integration with `brms`. Both `bmm` and `EMC2` specify designs with one formula per model parameter, but in `bmm` those are `brms` formulas: the random-effects syntax, the prior syntax, the post-processing ecosystem, and even non-linear formulas are the ones many researchers are already familiar with for mixed models. In addition, any grouping factor from the data can be used to specify random effects. So the lexical decision data analyzed below could carry by-word random effects alongside by-participant ones. `bmm` is also the only package that puts the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald approaches alongside the full DDM behind one interface, which is what makes the staged workflow of this tutorial possible: you can move between the three without rewriting your analysis. If your work sits in that mixed-model idiom, or spans several measurement models [@frischkorn2025tutorial; @frischkorn2026m3], `bmm` is the better fit.

## The `bmm` Workflow

Fitting any of the three models introduced above in `bmm` follows the same three steps:

1. Define the model: A model constructor function (`ezdm()`, `cswald()`, or `ddm()`) returns a model object carrying everything `bmm` needs to build the likelihood: which columns of your data hold the required response variables, and which model version should be specified and estimated.
2. Specify predictor formulas: The `bmmformula()` function, or its shorthand `bmf()`, defines how model parameters vary as a function of predictor variables (continuous or categorical) in the data. The syntax is the `brms` formula syntax [@burkner2017brms], including random effects.
3. Fit the model: Pass the model object, the formula, and the data to `bmm()`, which uses the provided information to translate the specification into a `brms` model and hands it to Stan for estimation.

All you have to provide is two things: how the variables required for the model are labeled in your data, and how parameters should vary over which conditions. `bmm` then does the rest: it provides the likelihood, fixes parameters a given version does not estimate, sets the link functions for proper sampling, chooses weakly informative default priors, and runs consistency checks on the data before fitting. In sum, the relationship between `bmm` and `brms` is the same as that between `brms` and Stan: each layer removes boilerplate from the one below without hiding it, and you can inspect either the brms objects generated by bmm or the stan code that was generated at any point.

One convention is worth stating before any of this: RTs must be coded in seconds, as they are in nearly all DDM software, because the parameters and their default priors are on that scale. `bmm` does not inspect or convert your RT scale, so data recorded in milliseconds must be divided by 1000 before fitting; otherwise ndt estimates and their priors will be badly mismatched.

As `bmm` builds on `brms`, fitted models can natively use almost all of the `brms` post-processing ecosystem: `summary()` provides an overview of the estimated model parameters and convergence diagnostics, `pp_check()` prints posterior predictive checks for every observable of the model's likelihood (selected with `resp_var`), `fixef()` and `ranef()` allows to extract posterior draws and summaries of parameter estimates, and the `hypothesis()` function enables testing non-linear hypotheses with support of Bayes Factors estimated via Savage-Dickey density ratios. Every tutorial below re-runs these same three steps with a different model object.

# Software and Data

All analyses run in R with `bmm` on the `cmdstanr` backend, which needs a working CmdStan installation (`cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()`). The packages loaded throughout are:

```{r}
#| label: setup-packages
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, cmdstanr, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork, rtdists)
```

All analyses use version 1.4.0 of `bmm`, available from CRAN via `install.packages("bmm")`.

# The Lexical Decision Dataset

To illustrate the functional capabilities of `bmm` with respect to DDM estimation, we use the classic lexical decision study by @wagenmakers2008lexical, available as `speed_acc` in the `rtdists` R package [@singmann2016rtdists].[^dataset] This dataset is ideal for a tutorial for several reasons: it is publicly available and widely used as a benchmark in the diffusion modeling literature, its experimental design has clear and well-tested EAM predictions, and published parameter estimates from the original analysis provide reference values for validating our results.

[^dataset]: The columns the tutorial uses are `id` (participant), `rt` (response time in seconds), `condition` (`speed` or `accuracy` emphasis), `stim_cat` (`word` or `nonword`), `frequency` (word frequency, recoded to the four-level `freq` factor in the companion script: `high`, `low`, `very_low`, and `nonword`), `response` (the key pressed, with `"error"` marking recording failures), and `censor` (trials the original study excluded).

In this experiment, 17 participants classified letter strings as words or nonwords under two instruction conditions: *speed emphasis* (respond as quickly as possible) and *accuracy emphasis* (respond as accurately as possible). Stimuli included words of varying frequency (high, low, very low) and matched nonwords, creating a 2 (emphasis) × 2 (stimulus category) within-subjects design with approximately 460 trials per cell per participant.

This design maps cleanly onto the selective influence principle introduced in the Background: emphasis should primarily affect bound, and stimulus category, and word frequency in particular, should primarily affect drift.

## Data Preparation

To prepare the data for DDM estimation, we first convert factors to character (needed because `response` and `stim_cat` have different factor level sets), and remove 6 recording failures and all trials flagged as `censor`, which are the trials the original study excluded. Note that the raw `response` column codes those recording failures with the level `"error"`: in `speed_acc` this means *no valid response was recorded*, not an incorrect response. Incorrect responses are identified later, by comparing `response` against `stim_cat`.^[The `censor` flag in the raw dataset is unrelated to the statistical *censoring* of error RTs used by the Censored-Shifted Wald in Part II. The companion script `scripts/01_prepare_lexical_data.R` contains the full data preparation code for this section.]

```{r}
#| label: data-load
data("speed_acc", package = "rtdists")

data_lexical <- speed_acc |>
  mutate(
    response = as.character(response),
    stim_cat = as.character(stim_cat),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("speed", "accuracy"))
  ) |>
  filter(response != "error", censor == FALSE)
```

For EAMs, the response variable must be binary, indicating which of the two decision boundaries was reached. Two codings are possible, each answering a different question:

- Accuracy-coding (upper = correct, lower = error): Drift reflects how quickly evidence for the *correct answer* accumulates. This is the standard approach for testing selective influence.
- Response-coding (upper = "word" response, lower = "nonword" response): Drift reflects evidence toward saying *"word"* specifically, positive for word stimuli, negative or near zero for nonwords. The relative starting point ($\zeta_r$) captures response bias toward saying "word."

```{r}
#| label: data-recode
# Accuracy-coded: correct = upper, error = lower
data_accuracy <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == stim_cat, "upper", "lower"))

# Response-coded: "word" response = upper, "nonword" response = lower
data_response <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == "word", "upper", "lower"))
```

# Data Preprocessing: Handling Contaminant Responses

In empirical data not all observed RTs arise from the evidence accumulation process that EAMs describe. Those that do not, the contaminants, violate the assumption that every RT is a decision time stemming from a DDM process plus a non-decision time [@ratcliff1993methods; @ratcliff2002estimating]. Premature responses, attentional lapses, and responses given without stimulus information are the usual sources. Even a few percent of such trials bias EAM parameter estimates. @ratcliff2008ez and @wagenmakers2008extensions both showed that contaminant RTs inflate the boundary separation the EZ-Diffusion Model recovers and distort its drift, and that the damage grows with the contamination rate. Preprocessing is therefore a neccessary step prior to estimating DDM parameters. The common approach, hard RT cutoffs that discard everything below or above fixed thresholds such as under 200 ms or above 3,000 ms, is arbitrary and often biased in its own right, because it can truncate legitimate fast and slow responses [@ulrich1994effects]. Simulation work on RT analysis more broadly reaches the same verdict: across a wide range of exclusion rules, the distortion the cure introduces often exceeds the one it removes [@berger2021outlier; @miller2023outlier]. `bmm` provides a model-based alternative that goes back to @ratcliff2002estimating and @wagenmakers2008extensions: a mixture model in which contaminant RTs follow a uniform distribution and the decision process follows a right-skewed core distribution, fitted per participant and condition.

## Identifying Contaminant Responses on the Trial Level

`flag_contaminant_rts()` fits the mixture within each cell you hand it. An expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm, which alternates between classifying trials and re-estimating the two components, decomposes the RT distribution into a core component and a uniform contaminant component and returns, for every trial, the probability under the fitted mixture that it is a contaminant. The core distribution can be ex-Gaussian, lognormal, or inverse Gaussian, all three right-skewed families commonly used to describe RT distributions; we use the ex-Gaussian, the sum of a normally and an exponentially distributed variable, which was the choice of @wagenmakers2008extensions. Applied to the accuracy-coded lexical decision data, grouped by participant, emphasis condition, and stimulus category, it appends one probability per trial:

```{r}
#| label: data-flag
data_accuracy <- data_accuracy |>
  group_by(id, condition, stim_cat) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt,
      distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

The `contaminant_bound` argument sets the support of the uniform component, here from the fastest to the slowest RT in the cell, which lets it absorb premature and delayed responses alike. When the EM does not converge in a cell, `flag_contaminant_rts()` warns and returns `NA` for every trial in that cell, and a filter on the probability then discards the whole cell. Check for `NA` in `contam_prob` before you filter, as the first line of the next chunk does: it stops with an error instead of letting a cell disappear. If the warning says the EM stopped at its iteration cap, raising `maxit` usually resolves it.

Trials with `contam_prob > 0.5` are more likely a contaminant than a legitimate response under the mixture, and the trial-level approaches of Part II exclude them:

```{r}
#| label: data-clean
stopifnot(!anyNA(data_accuracy$contam_prob))  # no cell may be dropped silently
data_accuracy_clean <- data_accuracy |> filter(contam_prob <= 0.5)
data_response_clean <- data_response |>
  semi_join(data_accuracy_clean, by = c("id", "condition", "stim_cat", "rt"))
```

The `semi_join()` keeps exactly those response-coded trials whose accuracy-coded counterpart survived. Both data frames thus contain the same trials, coded differently, and participant, condition, stimulus category, and RT serve as the matching key. The key is not unique, because RTs are recorded to the millisecond and many trials in a cell share one. Under the threshold rule it still matches correctly: the contaminant probability depends only on a trial's RT and its cell's fitted mixture, so trials that share a key are kept or dropped together, and the two cleaned data frames contain the same trials. A fixed threshold is the simplest rule and the easiest to report. The alternative, excluding each trial with probability equal to its contaminant probability, retains borderline trials in proportion to how uncertain their classification is; `scripts/01_prepare_lexical_data.R` applies the first and shows the second as a commented alternative, which needs a unique trial identifier for the join because it can separate tied trials. Where the flagged trials are fast, `validate_fast_guesses()` can be used to test whether they respond at chance, as premature responses should: given the flags, the RTs, and the responses, it returns a Bayes Factor for accuracy = 0.5 among the fast flagged trials.

## Computing Summary Statistics for the EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model does not require trial-level data. It takes, for every cell, the mean RT, the RT variance, the number of upper-boundary responses, and the number of trials, and `ezdm_summary_stats()` computes them. Its `method` argument selects how: `simple` returns the sample mean and variance; `robust` returns the median and a variance derived from the interquartile range, $(\mathrm{IQR}/1.349)^2$, where 1.349 is the IQR of a standard normal distribution, so the ratio estimates the SD (a MAD-based variant is available via `robust_scale`); and `mixture` fits the same uniform-plus-core mixture as `flag_contaminant_rts()` and returns the mean and variance of the fitted core distribution. The mixture method is the robust-EZ estimator of @wagenmakers2008extensions, and the robust method is the estimator @chavez2026robust proposed for the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model.[^robust-names]

[^robust-names]: The two names are easy to confuse. What @chavez2026robust call the "robust EZ-DDM" is the median/IQR method, `method = "robust"`; what @wagenmakers2008extensions call "robust-EZ" is the mixture method, `method = "mixture"`. They are different estimators.

We compute them from the contaminant-filtered trials, `data_accuracy_clean`, so that every fit in this tutorial, aggregated or trial-level, starts from the same trials; the mixture method then handles any contaminant the flags did not catch.

```{r}
#| label: data-sumstats
data_acc_ezdm <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(
      rt, response,
      version      = "3par",
      method       = "mixture",
      distribution = "exgaussian"
    ),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

`ezdm_summary_stats()` returns a one-row data frame for each cell, and `summarize()` spreads its columns into the result; `.by` groups for this one call without leaving the data grouped. `version = "3par"` pools both boundaries into one mean and one variance per cell, as the three-parameter model requires, whereas `"4par"` returns them separately for each boundary (Tutorial 2). The result has one row per participant × condition × stimulus category cell, with the columns `mean_rt`, `var_rt`, `n_upper`, and `n_trials` that `ezdm()` (Tutorial 1) expects, plus a `contaminant_prop` column with the proportion of contaminants the mixture estimated in each cell. Those four statistics are the entire input to the EZ-Diffusion Model. Everything else the raw trials contained is discarded, which is both why the approach is fast and why it cannot take trial-level predictors.

Under the mixture method the counts match the moments: `n_upper` and `n_trials` count the responses that the core distribution's mean and variance rest on, with the expected number of contaminants removed. Contaminants affect the proportion correct as well as the RT moments, because a response given without stimulus information is assumed to be correct only by chance. `ezdm_summary_stats()` therefore splits the removed contaminants across the two boundaries according to `guess_rate`, the accuracy expected of a contaminant response, which defaults to 0.5 for two response options. If the EM does not converge in a cell, `ezdm_summary_stats()` warns, returns the robust statistics for that cell instead, and sets `contaminant_prop` to `NA`; check that column for `NA` before fitting.

## Which Method to Use

I recommend the mixture method with the ex-Gaussian core as the default for `ezdm` preprocessing.
