It is the robust-EZ procedure of @wagenmakers2008extensions, which in their simulations was largely unaffected by contaminants where the standard moments were not. The robust statistics are the alternative when the EM cannot converge, which happens in cells with very few trials on one boundary (we hit exactly this case in Tutorial 2), or by preference: @chavez2026robust show that hypothesis tests on drift effects computed from the median and IQR are as accurate as tests from the standard moments on clean data and stay accurate under contamination. Their estimand is the drift-effect test, not the absolute parameter value. Because RT distributions are right-skewed, the median falls below the mean and the IQR-based variance below the variance, so the robust statistics carry an offset in absolute drift and bound that the mixture moments do not; the `bmm` documentation notes the same caveat. Hard cutoffs are not needed before either method, since the uniform component already spans both tails. The one place a lower cutoff earns its keep is before *trial-level* fitting, for a reason specific to those likelihoods that Part II explains. Absolute EAM parameter values are in any case not comparable across estimation procedures: the drift estimates we report below sit below the ones @wagenmakers2008lexical obtained from the same data, which came from a $\chi^2$ fit to quantile-averaged group data of a DDM that also estimated across-trial variability in drift, starting point, and non-decision time. What travels between studies are condition effects and individual differences.

# Part I: The EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model is the fastest of the three approaches by several orders of magnitude, and within `bmm` it is no longer the standalone calculator that @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion proposed. Recast as a likelihood over the three summary statistics of each cell [@chavez2025ez], it is a full Bayesian hierarchical model: population-level effects, arbitrary predictor structures via `bmf()`, random effects on any parameter, and shrinkage across participants. That addresses the two historical criticisms of the EZ approach, its sensitivity to contaminants, handled by the mixture preprocessing of the previous section, and its lack of a hierarchical structure [@ratcliff2008ez; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. What it keeps is the speed. Every fit in this part took seconds to minutes.

Part I makes the case for using it as a primary analysis. Tutorial 1 fits the three-parameter version to the accuracy-coded lexical decision data, tests condition effects on drift and bound, and then sharpens the stimulus contrast in a refit that costs a minute. Tutorial 2 switches to response coding and the four-parameter version to estimate the relative starting point. A parameter recovery study on simulated data with a biased starting point then shows what the four-parameter version buys and what fixing $\zeta_r$ at 0.5 costs, and closes with the timing contrast that motivates Part II.

## Tutorial 1: Exploring Condition Effects with the EZ-Diffusion Model

Let's start with the simplest and fastest DDM estimation approach in `bmm`: the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`). Because it fits in seconds rather than hours, it is the natural first step for exploring condition effects. The central question we address in this tutorial is: *Do speed–accuracy emphasis and stimulus category selectively influence different cognitive parameters?*^[The companion script `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` contains the full executable code for this tutorial.]

### Model Specification

Specifying an EAM in `bmm` involves two objects: a model object that defines the measurement model and maps data columns to model components, and a formula object that specifies the predictor structure for each parameter. The `ezdm()` function creates the model object:

```{r}
#| label: t1-model
#| eval: true
model_acc <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = "mean_rt",
  var_rt   = "var_rt",
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "3par"
)
```

The formula is specified using `bmf()`, which allows separate regression formulas for each parameter. We include stimulus category as a predictor on drift (to test for evidence quality differences) and emphasis condition as a predictor on bound (to test for response caution differences). Random slopes allow each participant's parameters to vary by condition: `(0 + stim_cat | id)` estimates participant-specific drift for words and nonwords, while `(0 + condition | id)` estimates participant-specific boundary settings under speed and accuracy emphasis. The `0 +` in these formulas suppresses the intercept, so the model estimates one coefficient per factor level, separate drifts for words and nonwords, separate bounds for speed and accuracy emphasis, rather than an intercept plus a difference. This makes the `fixef()` output below directly interpretable.

Each parameter uses a *link function* that determines how the linear predictor maps onto the parameter scale. Drift can take any real value, positive when evidence favors the upper boundary, negative when it favors the lower boundary, so it uses an *identity link*, meaning the regression coefficients are directly on the drift scale. Boundary separation and non-decision time, by contrast, must be strictly positive (a negative boundary or negative encoding time is meaningless), so they use a *log link*: the regression coefficients are on the log scale and must be exponentiated to obtain the parameter estimate. This is analogous to using a log link in Poisson regression to ensure predicted counts are positive. In practice, this means that when interpreting `fixef()` output, drift coefficients can be read directly, while bound and ndt coefficients require exponentiation (we demonstrate this below).

```{r}
#| label: t1-formula
#| eval: true
formula_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

We use `bmm`'s default priors throughout Tutorial 1. Before accepting any set of defaults it is worth seeing what they are, which `default_prior()` will tell you for any combination of formula, data, and model:

```{r}
#| label: t1-default-prior
default_prior(formula_acc, data_acc_ezdm, model_acc)
```

The output, printed by `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` (section 1), lists one prior per row. The `dpar` column identifies which model parameter each prior applies to, and `class` distinguishes population-level coefficients (`b`) from random-effect standard deviations (`sd`) and their correlations (`cor`). The row for `s` fixes the diffusion noise at 1 (a constant 0 on the log scale; see the Background), and the unlabeled constant row fixes the main `brms` parameter, which `bmm`'s DDM models do not use. Note that the priors on `bound` and `ndt` are stated on the log scale, matching their link functions, so a `normal(0, 0.5)` prior on `bound` is a prior over roughly 0.4 to 2.7 on the natural scale rather than over −1 to 1. Override any of them with `brms::prior()` (see Practical Guidelines).

If you do specify custom priors, verify that they produce plausible data before you look at your own: `bmm(..., sample_prior = "only")` samples from the prior alone, and `pp_check()` on the result shows you what RT distributions your priors imply. We skip that step here because the defaults are calibrated for typical RT data, but it is not optional once you depart from them [@schad2021principled].

### Model Fitting

To fit the model we call `bmm()`, which wraps `brms::brm()` with the model-specific likelihood. Setting `sample_prior = "yes"` stores prior samples, which the Savage-Dickey tests in the Hypothesis Testing section below require; `file` caches the fitted model to disk, so re-running the script does not re-fit it. `threads` splits each chain's likelihood evaluation across two cores, and the `control` arguments tune Stan's sampler: `adapt_delta` sets how cautiously the sampler takes steps (higher values mean smaller, safer steps) and `max_treedepth` caps how far a single step can travel. The values below are safe defaults for EAMs, and every subsequent tutorial reuses them.

```{r}
#| label: t1-fit
fit_acc_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm,
  model   = model_acc,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  threads = threading(2),
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc")
)
```

Every later fit reuses these sampler settings. Collected in a list, they can be passed to `bmm()` through `do.call()`, so that each later call names only what changes:

```{r}
#| label: t1-sampler
sampler <- list(
  chains = 5, cores = 5, threads = threading(2), warmup = 1000, iter = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr", sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12)
)
```

Fitting completed in `r t1_time` with five parallel chains. Convergence should always be verified before interpreting results. The two key diagnostics are $\hat{R}$ (which should be below 1.01 for all parameters) and effective sample size (ESS, which should be at least 400 for reliable posterior summaries). Both can be inspected via `summary(fit_acc_ezdm)`, which displays these diagnostics for every parameter. For this model, the maximum $\hat{R}$ was `r round(t1_rhat, 3)` and the minimum bulk ESS was `r round(t1_ess)`, indicating that the chains mixed well and the posterior was adequately sampled. Stan additionally reports divergent transitions, which `summary()` prints as a warning and `nuts_params()` counts; none of the fits in this tutorial produced any.^[If convergence issues arise, standard remedies include increasing the number of iterations, raising `adapt_delta` (e.g., to 0.95 or 0.99), or simplifying the random-effects structure. See the Troubleshooting section in Practical Guidelines for details.]

### Model Evaluation

Before interpreting parameter estimates, you should check whether the fitted model reproduces the data. For the EZ-Diffusion Model the data are three summary statistics per design cell, and `pp_check()` checks each of them. `pp_check_vars()` lists the observables a fitted model offers, and the `resp_var` argument selects one of them, or all of them at once:

```{r}
#| label: t1-ppcheck-code
pp_check_vars(fit_acc_ezdm)
pp_check(fit_acc_ezdm, resp_var = "all", ndraws = 50)
```

@fig-t1-ppcheck shows the three checks. Each panel compares how one statistic is distributed across the design cells, observed (dark) against the values simulated from the posterior (light): a density overlay for mean RT and RT variance, and binned bars for the proportion correct, which is bounded and takes few distinct values. Per-cell agreement is easier to count than to read off a density, so we also compare each cell with its own predictive interval (`pp_check(type = "intervals")`). A model that reproduced the cells would leave at most about one cell in ten outside its 90% interval. Here `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]` of the `r lex_cells` cells fall outside it for mean RT, `r t1_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]` for the RT variance, and `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` for the proportion correct. With hundreds of trials per cell the predictive intervals are narrow, so the checks are sensitive: they show where the cell statistics depart from what the formula allows, in which ndt is shared by all of a participant's cells, drift varies only with the two stimulus categories, and bound only with the two emphasis conditions. One caveat is specific to the EZ-Diffusion Model: because it is fit to three summary statistics per cell rather than to individual RTs, its checks can only show whether those statistics are reproduced, and cannot detect misfit in the finer shape of the RT distribution. The trial-level Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, which model individual RTs (including the separate distributions of correct and error responses), yield more diagnostic checks; we return to these in Part II.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Three-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Model"
#| apa-note: "Fit to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data, one panel per summary statistic: mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct. Each panel shows how one statistic is distributed across the participant × emphasis × stimulus-category cells: the observed distribution (dark) against 50 posterior draws (light), as a density overlay for mean RT and RT variance and as binned bars for the proportion correct."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_pp_check.pdf"))
```

Once model fit is evaluated, you can extract the population-level estimates with `fixef()`:

```{r}
#| label: t1-params
#| eval: true
fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
```

Read this table with the link functions for the respective parameters in mind. The two `drift_` rows use the identity link, so the `Estimate` column is already on the drift scale and can be read off directly. The `bound_` and `ndt_` rows use the log link, so their estimates are on the log scale and mean nothing until you exponentiate them. `Q2.5` and `Q97.5` bound the 95% credible interval, and they transform the same way — exponentiate the interval limits rather than trying to build an interval around the exponentiated mean.

```{r}
#| label: t1-params-transform
#| eval: true
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)[c("bound_conditionspeed", "bound_conditionaccuracy",
                          "ndt_Intercept"), ])
```

This is the step you will repeat for every log-link parameter in every model below, so it is worth doing explicitly once rather than reaching for a helper.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion Parameter Estimates From the Accuracy-Coded Analysis"
#| apa-note: "Top: drift by stimulus category. Bottom: bound by emphasis condition. Each panel shows the posterior density of the population-level estimate with its mean (point) and 66% and 95% credible intervals (thick and thin bars)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_param_estimates.pdf"))
```

The emphasis manipulation shows the expected effect on bound (@fig-t1-params): speed emphasis produced lower bound ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_speed`) than accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_acc`), reflecting reduced response caution. Drift estimates are nominally higher for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_word`) than nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_nonword`), but the difference is small; collapsing all words into a single category averages across high-, low-, and very-low-frequency items that differ strongly in drift, as the refit at the end of this tutorial shows. Non-decision time was estimated at $\tau$ = `r t1_ndt` seconds; this absolute value is specific to the estimation approach, and Part III shows how far the trial-level approaches sit from it. The bound result already demonstrates the core value of EAMs: a traditional analysis comparing mean RTs could not distinguish whether speed-emphasis participants were faster because they processed evidence more efficiently or because they required less evidence. We return to drift effects at the frequency level below, and Part III compares the result with the full DDM's at the same specification.

### Hypothesis Testing

Because we fitted the model with `sample_prior = "yes"`, we can use `brms::hypothesis()` to test hypotheses about the condition effects via Savage-Dickey density ratios. Writing a hypothesis as an equality (e.g., `drift_word = drift_nonword`) asks how much the data changed our belief in *no difference*: the resulting `Evid.Ratio` compares the posterior to the prior density at a difference of zero, and its inverse is the Bayes Factor (BF) quantifying the evidence *against* equality.^[With cell-means coding (`0 + condition`), no prior is placed on the difference itself; the prior `hypothesis()` uses for it is implied by the two level priors (their convolution, with $\sqrt{2}$ times the level SD), and it is centred at zero here because all levels share `bmm`'s default. The `bmm` hypothesis-testing vignette and @frischkorn2026m3 [Supplement 1] give the arithmetic and its consequences.] In other words, a BF of 10 means the data are ten times more likely under a model in which the two parameters differ than under one in which they are equal. As a rough guide, BFs above 3 indicate moderate evidence, above 10 strong evidence, and above 100 decisive evidence [@kass1995bayes]. All BFs reported in this tutorial follow this convention.

You can pass several hypotheses at once as a character vector, which keeps related tests together in one output table:

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis
# The seed makes the test reproducible: hypothesis() re-permutes the stored
# prior draws to build the implied prior on the tested difference
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
), seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
t1_hyp
```

The column to read is `Evid.Ratio`. For `bound` it is far below 1, so its inverse — the evidence against equality — is decisive (BF `r bf_fmt(t1_bf_bound)`): speed–accuracy emphasis unambiguously changes response caution. One caveat concerns precision. `hypothesis()` estimates the prior and the posterior density at zero from the draws, and with 5,000 posterior draws very large ratios are imprecise [@oberauerReliabilityBiasComputational2026], so we report them only as BF $\geq$ 10,000. The `seed` argument makes a test reproducible: the prior for a difference is built by re-permuting the stored prior draws, so without a seed the ratio changes slightly from call to call.

For `drift` the test comes out the other way. The BF against equality is `r round(t1_bf_drift, 2)`, meaning the data favor *no difference* between words and nonwords by roughly `r round(1 / t1_bf_drift)` to 1. This does not contradict the parameter estimates — words do show nominally higher drift — but it tells us the collapsed word/nonword contrast is too coarse to separate drift reliably. The next subsection revisits the contrast at the frequency level.

Two lessons follow, and both generalize beyond this dataset. Bayes Factors can quantify evidence *for* the absence of a difference, which a significance test cannot; and a selective influence test is only as sharp as the stimulus contrast you specify.

### Refining the Contrast: Word Frequency

The null result on drift invites a more refined test, and with the EZ-Diffusion Model an additional test is cheap. @wagenmakers2008lexical distinguished three word frequencies (high, low, very low) alongside nonwords, and the `freq` column carries that four-level factor. Recomputing the summary statistics per frequency level and substituting `freq` for `stim_cat` in the drift formula is the entire change to the model.[^recomputed-summary] The refit summarises the same contaminant-filtered trial-level data as the first fit, so the two fits differ only in the contrast. The new drift formula is:

[^recomputed-summary]: The summary statistics are recomputed with `.by = c(id, condition, freq)`, and the fit is the Tutorial 1 call with the formula specified here; `scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R` (section 1.1) contains both steps.

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq
formula_acc_freq <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

The fit for this slightly more complex model took `r t1f_time` and converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t1f_rhat, 3)`). The equality test on the two ends of the frequency scale settles the question the collapsed contrast could not:

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis
# A named hypothesis prints its name in place of the formula
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
           c(high_vs_very_low = "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low"),
           seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
# Printed as a data frame with the columns the text reads, so the table fits
# the page width; Evid.Ratio at full precision
print(t1f_hyp$hypothesis[, c("Hypothesis", "Estimate", "Est.Error",
                             "CI.Lower", "CI.Upper", "Evid.Ratio")],
      digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The posterior predictive check of the refit, run as for the first fit, leaves `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of the `r lex_cells_freq` cells outside their 90% intervals for mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct (Part III returns to what this misfit does and does not threaten). The evidence against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t1f_bf_drift)` (BF `r bf_fmt(t1f_bf_drift)`). Drift does vary with stimulus quality; the null result above was a property of how the stimulus contrast was specified, not of the parameter. The rank order the fit recovers is `r t1f_drift_order` (HF, LF, VLF: high-, low-, and very-low-frequency words; NW: nonwords), and Part III compares it with the full DDM's. Two lessons follow. A selective influence test is only as informative as the contrast you give it, and refining the contrast costs a minute with this model, which is what makes exploring the predictor structure with the EZ-Diffusion Model a habit worth forming before committing to a trial-level fit.

## Tutorial 2: Estimating Response Bias with the EZ-Diffusion Model (4par)

Tutorial 1 used accuracy coding, where "upper" means correct regardless of stimulus type. But what if we want to know whether participants are biased toward saying "word"? Response bias is a substantively important question in many domains: in lexical decision, word frequency creates an a priori expectation that biases responses toward "word"; in recognition memory, participants may adopt liberal or conservative response criteria; in clinical research, impulsive responding in ADHD may manifest as a shifted relative starting point rather than changed drift.

To estimate such biases you need two things: *response coding*, where "upper" always means a "word" response, and the 4-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm` 4par), which adds the relative starting point ($\zeta_r$) as a fourth parameter. The companion script for this tutorial is `scripts/12_tutorial2_ezdm_4par.R`.

### Model Specification

As introduced in the Data Preparation section, response coding changes the question the model answers — from "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward the *correct* answer?" to "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward saying *word*?" Drift is therefore positive for word stimuli and negative for nonwords. Bound and ndt retain their interpretations, but the key new parameter is the relative starting point $\zeta_r$: values above 0.5 indicate a tendency to say "word" before evidence accumulation has run its course, an *a priori response bias* that the accuracy-coded model could not detect.

The model object changes in two ways relative to Tutorial 1. Setting `version = "4par"` adds $\zeta_r$ to the estimated parameters, and `mean_rt` and `var_rt` now take a *pair* of column names rather than one each:

The four-parameter version needs the moments separately for each boundary. `version = "4par"` returns them as `mean_rt_upper`, `var_rt_upper`, `mean_rt_lower`, and `var_rt_lower`, and we use the robust statistics for the reason given under Trial-Count Constraint below:

```{r}
#| label: t2-data
data_resp_ezdm <- data_response_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par", method = "robust"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: t2-model
model_resp <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
  var_rt   = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "4par"
)
```

That pairing is what makes the fourth parameter identifiable. With an unbiased starting point, responses at the two boundaries have the same mean and variance; a starting point closer to one boundary makes responses at that boundary faster and less variable than responses at the other. The 4par version recovers $\zeta_r$ from exactly this asymmetry, which is why it needs boundary-specific moments where the 3par version needed only one mean and one variance per cell.

The formula adds one line for the new parameter, and is otherwise the Tutorial 1 formula:

```{r}
#| label: t2-formula
formula_resp_ezdm <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

Note that $\zeta_r$ is written `zr` in the formula, and that it gets emphasis condition as a predictor: this asks whether participants shift their starting point when instructed to favor speed over accuracy.

### Model Fitting

Fitting uses the Tutorial 1 call, with the response-coded summary statistics, the 4par model object, and the `sampler` list:

```{r}
#| label: t2-fit
fit_resp_ezdm <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_resp_ezdm, data = data_resp_ezdm, model = model_resp,
  file = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp")), sampler))
```

### Model Evaluation

Convergence was adequate (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2_rhat, 3)`). The posterior predictive checks (@fig-t2-ppcheck) follow Tutorial 1, now with mean RT and RT variance separately for "word" and "nonword" responses and the proportion of "word" responses. Depending on the statistic, between `r min(t2_ppc_out)` and `r max(t2_ppc_out)` of the `r t2_cells` cells fall outside their 90% intervals, so the four-parameter version leaves systematic misfit in the cell statistics as well.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Four-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Model"
#| apa-note: "Fit to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Panels show mean RT and RT variance for word and nonword responses, and the proportion of word responses. Each panel shows how one statistic is distributed across the design cells: the observed distribution (dark) against 50 posterior draws (light), as a density overlay for the RT statistics and as binned bars for the proportion of word responses."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_pp_check.pdf"))
```

As expected, drift reverses by stimulus category: positive for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_word`, evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary) and negative for nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_nonword`, evidence accumulates toward the "nonword" boundary). This sign reversal is a direct consequence of response coding; the same underlying evidence accumulation process is now expressed relative to the "word" boundary rather than the "correct" boundary. The $\zeta_r$ estimates, back-transformed with `plogis()` from the logit scale on which `fixef()` reports them, reveal a small starting-point shift: $\zeta_r$ = `r t2_zr_acc_ci` under accuracy emphasis and $\zeta_r$ = `r t2_zr_speed_ci` under speed emphasis. The accuracy-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_acc` suggests a slight bias toward saying "word," while the speed-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_speed` is close to unbiased. The original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis reported $\zeta_r$ = 0.497 for accuracy and 0.476 for speed. Our estimates do not reproduce those values; the accuracy-emphasis interval lies above 0.5, where the published value sits just below it. What the two analyses share is the size of the deviation: both place the starting point within 0.03 of 0.5, a very small a priori response bias (@fig-t2-params).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-params
#| fig-cap: "Four-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Estimates From the Response-Coded Analysis"
#| apa-note: "Top: drift by stimulus category, positive for word stimuli and negative for nonword stimuli (evidence toward the word boundary). Bottom: relative starting point by emphasis condition; the dashed line marks 0.5, an unbiased starting point. Each panel shows the posterior density of the population-level estimate with its mean (point) and 66% and 95% credible intervals (thick and thin bars)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_resp_params.pdf"))
```

### Hypothesis Testing

Equality tests analogous to Tutorial 1 confirm the expected patterns. The Bayes Factors against zero drift for words (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_word)`) and for nonwords (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_nw)`), and against equal bound across emphasis conditions (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_bound)`), are all decisive. The selective influence pattern is robust to the change in response coding.

The four-parameter version also makes the starting point itself testable, which is what decides between the three- and four-parameter versions on a given dataset. The point hypothesis `zr_conditionaccuracy = 0` on the logit scale is $\zeta_r$ = 0.5, an unbiased starting point. The Bayes factor against it is BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_zr_acc)` under accuracy emphasis and BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_zr_speed)` under speed emphasis, where values below 1 favour an unbiased starting point. This is a nested comparison, a point restriction on one parameter of a single fitted model, and the Savage-Dickey ratio is the tool for it; comparing specifications that differ in more than that is a different question (Practical Guidelines).

### Trial-Count Constraint

One practical limitation surfaced in this analysis, and it matters beyond this dataset. The `ezdm` 4par version requires enough trials on *both* boundaries in every cell. In this dataset, nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses — median `r t2_minority_median` per cell, minimum `r t2_minority_min` — which makes the variance estimate for the minority boundary unreliable. `ezdm_summary_stats()` returns `NA` moments for a boundary with fewer than `min_trials` responses (10 by default). Such a boundary does not cost the cell its place in the fit: `bmm` keeps the cell and lets that boundary enter through its response counts alone, so it still speaks to accuracy but says nothing about the shape of the minority-boundary RT distribution. Here `r t2_cells_counts_only` of the `r t2_cells` cells entered that way. Dropping these cells instead would remove precisely the cells with the most extreme accuracy. This is not a quirk of our preprocessing; it arises organically whenever a condition is easy enough that participants rarely err, and it is why we computed the 4par summary statistics with `method = "robust"` rather than `method = "mixture"`: the mixture method's EM step cannot converge on a cell containing a single observation.

The constraint is not merely a technical inconvenience. It points at a general limitation of summary-statistic approaches: when a cell contains very few responses on one boundary, the per-cell moments that the EZ-Diffusion Model requires stop being estimable, and no amount of care in preprocessing recovers them. Trial-level approaches sidestep the problem entirely, because they never form per-cell statistics: they evaluate a likelihood for each observation and borrow strength across participants through the hierarchical structure. Part II returns to them. Before that, the next section asks a question the lexical decision data cannot answer, because their starting point sits so close to 0.5: what does the four-parameter version buy when the starting point is in fact biased?

## Recovering a Biased Starting Point

The three-parameter model fixes $\zeta_r$ at 0.5. The lexical decision data barely test that assumption, because the estimated starting points sit within a few hundredths of 0.5 under both emphasis conditions. Many designs are less forgiving. Unequal stimulus proportions, payoff manipulations, and prior expectations all shift the starting point, and a model that fixes it has to absorb the shift elsewhere. To see what the four-parameter version buys under such conditions, and what ignoring the bias costs, I simulated data with a known, biased starting point and fitted both versions alongside the full DDM.

### Design

Fifty simulated participants completed a two-choice task with two stimulus types and two bias conditions (data columns `stimulus` and `bias`), `r bias_trials_per_cell` trials per cell. The stimulus type sets the direction of drift, positive for stimulus A and negative for stimulus B, so that with response coding (upper = an "A" response) both boundaries are reached often. The bias condition sets the relative starting point at 0.60 (toward the "A" boundary) or 0.40 (toward the "B" boundary). Bound (1.5) and non-decision time (0.3 s) did not vary by condition. Participant-level parameters were drawn around these population values with between-participant standard deviations of 0.25 on drift, 0.15 on log bound, 0.03 s on ndt, and 0.20 on the logit of $\zeta_r$; the drift spread is smaller than in the appendix's recovery study so that every cell keeps enough responses at its minority boundary for the boundary-specific moments the four-parameter model needs. I then fitted the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model with a bias-condition effect on $\zeta_r$, the three-parameter model to the same cells with $\zeta_r$ fixed at 0.5, and the full DDM with the four-parameter formula:

```{r}
#| label: bias-formula
formula_bias <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stimulus + (0 + stimulus | id),
  bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + bias + (0 + bias | id)
)
```

### Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Group-Level Recovery With a Biased Starting Point"
#| apa-note: "Points are posterior means with 95% credible intervals for the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (starting point fixed at 0.5), and the full DDM; dashed lines mark the generating values. Panels show drift by stimulus type, bound, non-decision time, and the relative starting point by bias condition. Bound did not meet the convergence criteria in any of the three fits (see text); only the starting point is interpreted."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
if (bias_ok) {
  knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "22_bias_recovery_group.pdf"))
} else {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Figure pending: scripts/22_bias_recovery.R has not been run yet.") + theme_void()
}
```

@fig-bias-recovery shows the group-level estimates against the generating values. The four-parameter model estimated $\zeta_r$ = `r bias_zr_A` under the A-bias condition and `r bias_zr_B` under the B-bias condition, against generating values of 0.60 and 0.40; the full DDM estimated `r bias_ddm_zr_A` and `r bias_ddm_zr_B`. None of the three fits met the convergence criteria of the Practical Guidelines for the population-level bound (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r bias_bound_rhat_max`, minimum bulk ESS = `r bias_bound_ess_min`), and the full DDM also fell short of the ESS criterion for drift and ndt. Because the parameters of one fit share a joint posterior, we interpret only the starting point, whose diagnostics passed in both models that estimate it; the remaining estimates appear in @fig-bias-recovery and in the subject-level scatter plots of the appendix for completeness and are not interpreted. At the subject level, recovered $\zeta_r$ correlated with the generating values at $r$ = `r bias_r_zr_min` to `r bias_r_zr_max` in both models.

The fits took `r bias_time_4par` (four-parameter EZ-Diffusion), `r bias_time_3par` (three-parameter), and `r bias_time_ddm` (full DDM). That contrast, at most around 2 minutes for each EZ-Diffusion fit against hours for the full DDM on the same 50 participants, is the reason Part II fits the trial-level approaches once, at a specification the EZ-Diffusion Model has already explored, rather than developing the model at trial-level cost.


# Part II: Trial-Level Estimation

## Tutorial 3: The Censored-Shifted Wald and the Full DDM at the Same Specification

So far the EZ-Diffusion Model has worked with three summary statistics per cell. Trial-level modeling preserves the shape of the RT distribution, allows trial-level predictors, and handles sparse cells through hierarchical shrinkage rather than through per-cell variance estimates. The price is a likelihood evaluated for every trial. `bmm` offers two trial-level approaches. The Censored-Shifted Wald replaces the two-boundary process with one or two single-boundary shifted Wald accumulators [@anders2016shifted; @heathcote2004fitting], and its simple version is the only trial-level fit that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM (Part III reports the timings). The full DDM evaluates the Wiener first-passage time distribution, with its infinite series, for every trial; it is the mathematically complete characterization of the process and the reference against which the other approaches are judged. This tutorial fits both, together with the competing-risks version of the Censored-Shifted Wald, at the specification Part I arrived at, four frequency levels on drift, so that Part III can compare the three approaches parameter by parameter. The companion scripts are `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` and `scripts/14_tutorial4_ddm.R`.

The `bmm` workflow is unchanged. What differs from Part I is the model object (`cswald()` or `ddm()` instead of `ezdm()`) and the data: the trial-level `rt` and `response` columns instead of aggregated summary statistics. The `response` column must contain the values `"upper"` and `"lower"`, identifying which boundary each trial reached, which is the coding applied in the Data Preparation section.

### Preparing Trial-Level Data

The cleaned trial-level data from the Data Preprocessing section are the input. One property of the trial-level likelihoods concerns which trials should be in the data at all. Both the shifted Wald density and the Wiener density are zero for any RT shorter than the non-decision time. A trial faster than ndt therefore does not merely fit poorly; it has no likelihood, and the sampler responds by forcing ndt below the fastest surviving RT, with bound and drift absorbing the consequences. Under the simple Censored-Shifted Wald an *error* faster than ndt behaves differently. It contributes the log survival function, which at an RT below ndt equals zero, the largest value that term can take, and so pushes ndt upward. The mixture flags of `flag_contaminant_rts()` do not target this region, because the EM knows nothing about ndt; what removes such trials is a lower RT cutoff. The lexical decision data already carry one, since `censor == FALSE` applies the original study's bounds of 180 ms and 3 s, and the fastest RT in the cleaned data is `r min_rt_ms` ms. If your own data do not, apply a lower cutoff before any trial-level fit, at a value below any plausible non-decision time for your task, and leave the slow tail to the mixture flags.

Before comparing estimates against published ones, one point about the scale of DDM parameters needs stating, because it silently invalidates comparisons that ignore it. DDM parameters are defined only relative to a scaling constant: multiplying drift, bound, and the diffusion noise $s$ by the same factor leaves the predicted data unchanged. `bmm` and Stan fix $s = 1$, whereas older software often used $s = 0.1$. Reference values drawn from that older literature must therefore be rescaled, by a factor of 10, before they can be compared with `bmm` output. All reference values we quote below have been converted to $s = 1$.

### Model Specification

The Censored-Shifted Wald model object needs the RT column, the response column, and the version. The *simple* version treats errors as censored observations, in the sense set out in the Background: each error tells the model only that the correct-boundary process had not finished by the observed RT. Because censored trials constrain the parameters less than completed ones, this version needs errors to stay reasonably rare, and @miller2018shifted put the guideline at 20%. The lexical decision data test that guideline once the four frequency levels are separated. Accuracy-coded error rates run from `r err_min`% (high-frequency words under accuracy emphasis) to `r err_second`% (low-frequency words under speed emphasis) in seven of the eight emphasis × frequency cells, and reach `r err_max`% for very-low-frequency words under speed emphasis. We keep the frequency specification for comparability with the other two approaches, and Part III reports whether the approximation's known weak point, the boundary estimate, deviates more in that cell.

The *competing-risks* (crisk) version models errors explicitly: two accumulators race, one per response boundary, sharing a single non-decision time, and whichever finishes first produces the observed response. Nothing is left as a lower bound, which is what allows this version to estimate the relative starting point $\zeta_r$, and it carries no error-rate guideline. We apply it to the response-coded data, where it can estimate $\zeta_r$ and handle the unbalanced boundary counts that limited the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach.

The full DDM's model object is the simplest of the three. `ddm()` needs only the RT and response columns; there is no `version` argument, because the full DDM has one form, and $\zeta_r$ is included or omitted by whether the formula supplies a `zr` line. The three model objects are:

```{r}
#| label: t3-models
model_simple <- cswald(rt = "rt", response = "response", version = "simple")
model_crisk  <- cswald(rt = "rt", response = "response", version = "crisk")
model_ddm    <- ddm(rt = "rt", response = "response")
```

Two formulas serve all four fits. For the accuracy-coded analysis, all drifts are positive: they measure evidence toward the correct boundary regardless of stimulus type. A consequence worth anticipating is that the drift rank order differs from the response-coded model. High-frequency words have the highest drift, but nonwords, which are relatively easy to reject, have higher drift than very-low-frequency words, which are difficult to recognize. The expected rank order from @wagenmakers2008lexical is HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > NW (2.64) > VLF (1.80). The formula is the one of the frequency refit in Tutorial 1, passed unchanged to the simple Censored-Shifted Wald and to the full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-acc
formula_trial_acc <- formula_acc_freq
```

For the response-coded analysis, drift sign reflects the stimulus: positive for words, where evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary, and negative for nonwords. The expected values are HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > VLF (1.80) > 0 > NW (−2.64). Adding a `zr` line lets $\zeta_r$ capture any bias toward saying "word"; the reference values suggest a very small shift between conditions ($\zeta_r$ = 0.497 accuracy, 0.476 speed). This formula is passed to the competing-risks version and to the full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-resp
formula_trial_resp <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

### Model Fitting

The four calls differ only in formula, data, model object, and output file; the sampler settings are those of Part I, and every fit in this tutorial ran with two threads per chain, one fit at a time, so that the timings Part III reports are comparable across approaches (see the note to @tbl-model-comparison). All four pass the `sampler` list of Tutorial 1:

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit
fit_cswald_simple <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_acc, data = data_accuracy_clean, model = model_simple,
  file = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple")), sampler))
fit_cswald_crisk <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_crisk,
  file = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp")), sampler))
fit_ddm_acc <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_acc, data = data_accuracy_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc")), sampler))
fit_ddm_resp <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp")), sampler))
```

We set `adapt_delta = 0.90` and `max_treedepth = 12` for both the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM to reduce divergent transitions and max-treedepth warnings. If you fit trial-level models of your own, start from these values rather than the `brms` defaults.

### Model Evaluation

All four models converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_simple, 3)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, `r round(t3_rhat_crisk, 3)` for the competing-risks version, `r round(t4_rhat_acc, 3)` and `r round(t4_rhat_resp, 3)` for the accuracy- and response-coded DDM). The posterior predictive checks (@fig-trial-ppcheck) cover the three observables of the trial-level likelihoods: the RT distribution, the response proportions, and the signed RT, which places lower-boundary responses on the negative axis and so checks choices and RTs jointly. Unlike the checks in Part I, they can show misfit in the shape of the distribution, because these models are fitted to individual RTs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trial-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Four Trial-Level Fits"
#| apa-note: "Fits to the Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data: the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (accuracy-coded), the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald (response-coded), and the full DDM under both codings. One row per fit; the columns show the response time, the response (lower = 0, upper = 1), and the signed response time (lower-boundary responses negative). Dark: observed data; light: data simulated from 50 posterior draws. For the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, the response and signed-RT panels reflect its censored likelihood, which does not generate errors at the observed rate (see text)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
if (file.exists(here("figures", "15_pp_check_trial_level.pdf"))) {
  knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_pp_check_trial_level.pdf"))
} else {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Figure pending: scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R produces the composite check after the refit.") + theme_void()
}
```

The response panel of the first row shows what the censored likelihood of the simple version cannot reach. The observed data contain `r t3s_pp_lower[["obs"]]` lower-boundary responses, the errors; data simulated from the fitted simple model contain `r t3s_pp_lower[["pred"]]` on average, because errors enter that likelihood only as censored correct responses, and the two-boundary process the simulation runs with the fitted drift and the doubled bound rarely terminates at the error boundary. That panel is not a test of fit but a reminder of what the simple version does not model; its RT panel is the informative one. The full DDM does generate errors, but fewer than observed (`r t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]]` against `r t4a_pp_lower[["obs"]]`), a shortfall the per-cell comparison in Part III returns to.

One point about scale is relevant before checking the estimates, because it is easy to forget. The simple version has only one boundary, and what it estimates as bound is the distance from the starting point to that boundary. With an unbiased starting point this is *half* the boundary separation that `ezdm` and `ddm` report, so `cswald(version = "simple")` estimates must be multiplied by 2 before they are compared with the other two approaches or with published values. We do so throughout, and the scripts apply the same factor. The conversion is a matter of definition, not of accuracy. On data simulated from a known diffusion process, fitting the `bmm` simple likelihood returns a bound close to half the generating separation, as the definition predicts, but the doubled estimate is not thereby an unbiased estimate of $\alpha$: bound is the parameter the single-boundary approximation has the weakest claim on, because collapsing two boundaries into one is precisely an assumption about the boundaries. The crisk version needs no conversion; it estimates the full separation directly.

Extracting the estimates follows Tutorial 1, with two additions for the simple version: its drift is on the log link, and its bound is the single-boundary distance, so both are exponentiated and the bound is doubled. The competing-risks $\zeta_r$ is back-transformed with `plogis()`. Section 3.3 of `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` applies these transformations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trial-estimates
#| tbl-cap: "Part II Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale. Accuracy-coded rows compare the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (bound doubled to the full-boundary scale, drift exponentiated from the log link) with the accuracy-coded full DDM; the $\\zeta_r$ rows compare the competing-risks version with the response-coded full DDM."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
.g <- function(fe, row, f = identity, d = 2, m = 1)
  fmt_est(f(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * m, d)
.lv <- c(high = "HF", low = "LF", very_low = "VLF", nonword = "NW")
trial_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c(paste0("Drift ($\\delta$), ", .lv), "Bound ($\\alpha$), speed",
                "Bound ($\\alpha$), accuracy", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)",
                "$\\zeta_r$, speed", "$\\zeta_r$, accuracy"),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald` = c(
    purrr::map_chr(names(.lv), \(l) .g(fe_t3s, paste0("drift_freq", l), exp)),
    .g(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed", exp, m = 2), .g(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy", exp, m = 2),
    .g(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", exp, 3),
    .g(fe_t3c, "zr_conditionspeed", plogis, 3), .g(fe_t3c, "zr_conditionaccuracy", plogis, 3)),
  `Full DDM` = c(
    purrr::map_chr(names(.lv), \(l) .g(fe_t4a, paste0("drift_freq", l))),
    .g(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed", exp), .g(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy", exp),
    .g(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", exp, 3),
    .g(fe_t4r, "zr_conditionspeed", plogis, 3), .g(fe_t4r, "zr_conditionaccuracy", plogis, 3))
)
knitr::kable(trial_tab, align = "lcc")
```

@tbl-trial-estimates collects the population-level estimates of the four fits (`scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R`, section 3.4, plots the posteriors). Both trial-level approaches recover the drift sign reversal seen in the EZ-Diffusion 4par. The competing-risks version also handled without complaint the sparse minority-boundary cells that forced the EZ-Diffusion 4par onto the robust aggregation method: because it evaluates a likelihood per trial rather than moments per cell, a cell with one "word" response is simply a cell with one observation.

### Hypothesis Testing

As in Part I, we quantify the evidence with equality tests. The Bayes Factor against equal bound across emphasis conditions is `r bf_label(t4_bf_bound)` for the full DDM (BF `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_bound)`) and `r bf_label(t3_bf_bound)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (BF `r bf_fmt(t3_bf_bound)`), reproducing the conclusion Part I reached in seconds. The full DDM's Bayes Factor against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t4_bf_drift)` (BF `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_drift)`), the same verdict the EZ-Diffusion refit of Tutorial 1 returned in a minute.

### When to Use Which Version

Use the simple version when error rates are low, below roughly 20%, and your research question does not require the relative starting point. On the lexical decision data it kept the word-frequency ordering of drift, but its drift estimates ran `r simple_drift_lo`% to `r simple_drift_hi`% above the full DDM's, and its bound, even after the factor of 2 described above, ran `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% to `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above (Part III). It is the only version of the Censored-Shifted Wald that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM. Use the competing-risks version when error rates are higher, when $\zeta_r$ is of interest, or when response coding is used. It costs most of what the full DDM costs, so it is a choice about what you want to estimate rather than a way to save time. On these data its estimates were close to the full DDM's, bound included, which differed by at most `r bound_crisk_diff`%; on the simulated data of the appendix, however, it placed bound `r rec_crisk_bound_pct`% below the generating value, where the full DDM recovered it. The simple version's bound, then, is not an absolute value to take at face value. The direction of the boundary effect was the same under every approach in our analyses (Part III), so questions about the *direction* of a boundary effect are safe; if your question concerns its precise magnitude, prefer the full DDM.

# Part III: Comparison and Practical Guidelines

## Cross-Approach Comparison

Having applied all three DDM estimation approaches to the same dataset at the same specification, we can answer a question that is difficult to answer without a unified framework: does the EZ-Diffusion Model reach the full DDM's conclusions, and where do the approximations break down or diverge? Agreement validates the faster approaches against the reference; disagreement shows where the computational savings come at a substantive cost.

For this comparison, I considered reaching "the same conclusions" as follows: for every condition effect, the approaches agree on its sign, on the rank order of the condition levels, and on the evidence category of the Bayes factor against equality [anecdotal, moderate, strong, or decisive; @kass1995bayes]. Absolute parameter values are not part of the criterion; the comparison reports them, and they differ. Two limits of the evidence belong at the outset as well. The effects tested in all three approaches are large, with Bayes factors beyond the resolution of the posterior sample, so no effect tested across approaches was small enough for them to disagree; and non-decision time carried no predictor in any fit, so agreement was never evaluated for it. We start with the cost, because it is what the comparison is for.

### Computational Cost

The fitting times on the present dataset span three orders of magnitude. The EZ-Diffusion fits took `r cost_ezdm_range`, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald `r cost_cswald_simple`, the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald `r cost_cswald_crisk`, and the full DDM `r cost_ddm_range` (wall-clock of the slowest of five parallel chains, two threads per chain, one fit at a time). Two features of this hierarchy matter for how the approaches should be used. First, the EZ-Diffusion Model provides in minutes what takes the full DDM the better part of a day: for the accuracy-coded frequency specification the factor is `r cost_factor`. That factor is not a constant of the approaches. The EZ-Diffusion likelihood is evaluated once per design cell, `r lex_cells_freq` times here, the trial-level likelihoods once per trial, `r format(nrow(data_accuracy_clean), big.mark = ",")` times, so the saving grows with the number of trials per cell and shrinks with the number of cells: a design with more trials and fewer cells saves more than reported here, one with many sparse cells less. The timings also come from one machine (see the note to @tbl-model-comparison). Second, the computational saving of the Censored-Shifted Wald lies mainly in its simple version, which took `r cost_simple_share`% of the accuracy-coded full DDM's time. The competing-risks version took `r cost_crisk_share`% of the response-coded full DDM's time, so it should be chosen for what it estimates, a relative starting point at higher error rates, not for speed.

### Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-Approach Comparison of Accuracy-Coded Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Estimates at the four-level frequency specification. Panels show drift by word-frequency level, bound by emphasis condition, and non-decision time for the EZ-Diffusion Model, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (bound converted to the full-boundary scale), and the full DDM. Error bars show 95% credible intervals; X markers show the reference values of Wagenmakers et al. (2008), rescaled to s = 1."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded estimates side by side. All three approaches converge on the same substantive picture: emphasis changes bound in the same direction, and drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels, in the same order for the three word levels (high > low > very low). Low-frequency words and nonwords sit close together in all three, and the full DDM places nonwords marginally above low-frequency words. The conclusions hold whether the model consumed summary statistics (EZ-Diffusion), a single-boundary approximation (Censored-Shifted Wald), or the full Wiener likelihood (DDM).

Where the approaches diverge, they diverge in absolute values (@tbl-cross-model-acc reports the parameters all three share). The EZ-Diffusion Model's drift estimates differ from the full DDM's by `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% on average (`r t4_drift_pct_lo`% to `r t4_drift_pct_hi`% across frequency levels). Relative to known generating values, EZ-Diffusion drift is *attenuated* at high values when trial-to-trial variability is present [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; relative to the full DDM fitted to the same empirical data, it ran at or above the DDM's here, most for high-frequency words. What matters for practice is that the condition differences keep their sign and order. For bound, once the simple Censored-Shifted Wald estimates are put on the full-boundary scale, the three approaches order themselves the same way under both emphasis conditions: the EZ-Diffusion Model lowest, the full DDM in between, and the simple Censored-Shifted Wald highest. The simple version sits `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% above the full DDM under accuracy emphasis and `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above under speed emphasis. Speed emphasis contains the one cell above the 20% error guideline, very-low-frequency words at `r err_max`% errors, but bound is estimated per emphasis condition, so the fit cannot attribute the larger deviation to that cell. Drift is estimated per frequency level, and there the cell does leave a trace: the simple version's drift exceeded the full DDM's most for very-low-frequency words, the level that contains it. The EZ-Diffusion Model sits `r bound_ez_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez_deficit["speed"]`% below the full DDM. Its values lie nearest the published ones (1.59 and 0.84), but those come from a different estimation procedure (Which Method to Use), so the proximity is not evidence that it estimates bound more accurately. Non-decision time was estimated at `r t4_ndt_ez` s by the EZ-Diffusion Model, `r t4_ndt_ddm` s by the full DDM, and `r t3s_ndt` s by the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, against a published 0.408 s; the Limitations section returns to why the trial-level estimates sit lower.

All of these divergences concern the absolute parameter scale. On the two questions applied work asks, does the manipulation change the parameter, and do individuals differ from one another, the approaches agree.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-Coded Estimates of the Parameters the Three Approaches Share"
#| apa-note: "Posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale, for bound by emphasis condition and ndt. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. The EZ-Diffusion column is the frequency refit of Tutorial 1, so its bound differs slightly from the first fit's. Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) bound estimates are multiplied by 2 to convert them from the single-boundary scale to the full boundary separation the other two approaches report."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2, m = 1) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * m, d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

### Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-Approach Comparison of Response-Coded Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Left: drift by word-frequency level; all three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Middle: bound by emphasis condition. Right: relative starting point by emphasis condition; all three approaches estimate values close to 0.5. Error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_response.pdf"))
```

The response-coded comparison (@fig-comparison-resp) evaluates whether the approaches agree on two patterns: the drift sign reversal by stimulus category and the starting-point shift under speed emphasis. All three approaches recover the expected drift pattern, positive for word stimuli, negative for nonwords, so the response-coding interpretation is robust across estimation approaches. The relative starting point $\zeta_r$ estimates are close to 0.5 across approaches and emphasis conditions, consistent with the small bias reported in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis. In bound, the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald agreed with the full DDM to within `r bound_crisk_diff`%, while the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model placed it `r bound_ez4_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez4_deficit["speed"]`% lower, as the three-parameter version did under accuracy coding. Part of that gap is the aggregation method rather than the approach. The four-parameter statistics were computed with the robust method, whose median and IQR-based variance sit below the mean and variance of a right-skewed RT distribution (Data Preprocessing). Refitting the same `r ez4f_cells` cells from mixture moments, with the EM falling back to the robust statistics for `r mix_fallback$boundaries_fallback` of the `r 2 * mix_fallback$cells` boundaries (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2fm_rhat, 3)`), places bound `r bound_ez4mix_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez4mix_deficit["speed"]`% below the full DDM's. The `r bound_ez4_offset_pts["accuracy"]` and `r bound_ez4_offset_pts["speed"]` percentage points between the two fits are what the aggregation method contributes; the rest of the gap is the approach, as under accuracy coding, where the three-parameter fit used mixture moments throughout. The four-parameter fit at this specification rests on sparse cells: with the robust method and `min_trials = 3`, `r ez4f_cells_counts_only` of the `r ez4f_cells` cells (17 participants × 2 emphasis conditions × 4 frequency levels) have a boundary with no usable RT summaries and enter through their response counts alone, and among the remainder some estimate a boundary's variance from three responses.

The comparison also answers a question the posterior predictive checks of Part I left open. The EZ-Diffusion fits left `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of `r lex_cells` cells outside their 90% intervals for mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct, and the frequency refit `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of `r lex_cells_freq`. Those checks are sensitive because hundreds of trials per cell make the predictive intervals narrow, and they show that the per-cell statistics depart from what a formula with one ndt per participant and one bound per emphasis condition allows. What the comparison adds is twofold. First, the full DDM, fitted to the individual trials at the same specification, reaches the same sign, order, and evidence category for every condition effect. Second, put through the same per-cell check from the same number of posterior draws (@tbl-ppc-cells), the trial-level fits miss at least as many cells: the accuracy-coded full DDM leaves `r .tp_count("Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "mean_rt")`, `r .tp_count("Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "var_rt")`, and `r .tp_count("Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "p_upper")` of the `r lex_cells_freq` cells outside their intervals for mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct, against `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` for the EZ-Diffusion refit, and the RT variance is where every trial-level fit misses most. The misfit therefore belongs to the specification the three approaches share, one bound per emphasis condition, one ndt per participant, and no trial-to-trial variability, not to the aggregation into summary statistics; and it sits in the absolute values and in how parameters are shared across cells, not in the contrasts. A reader who needs every cell reproduced needs a richer specification, not a different estimation approach; a reader who needs condition effects has them from any of the three.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppc-cells
#| tbl-cap: "Design Cells Outside Their 90% Posterior Predictive Interval"
#| apa-note: "Cells (of 136: participant × emphasis × frequency level) whose observed mean RT, RT variance, or proportion of upper-boundary responses falls outside its 90% posterior predictive interval, for the EZ-Diffusion frequency refit and the four trial-level fits, each from 50 posterior draws. For the simple Censored-Shifted Wald the proportion column is not a test of fit, because its censored likelihood does not generate errors (Part II)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(ppc_cells_tab, align = "lccc")
```

Taken together, the comparison supports the position Part I argued for. For research questions about drift and about the direction of effects on bound and $\zeta_r$, the EZ-Diffusion Model is a primary analysis, not a screening step. When the absolute values of bound or $\zeta_r$ are themselves the quantity of interest, or when the shape of the RT distribution is itself the question, the full DDM is preferable, with the simple Censored-Shifted Wald as the affordable trial-level middle ground for high-accuracy data.

## Practical Guidelines

This part delivers the fourth learning objective: deciding which approach a question needs, and reading the differences between them.

### Things to Keep in Mind

Before the approach-specific recommendations, here are the requirements and conventions that apply whichever approach you use. Most of them have caused us or our students trouble at some point.

- RTs must be in seconds. `bmm` does not inspect or convert your RT scale, and the default priors on ndt assume seconds. If your data are in milliseconds, divide by 1000 before fitting.
- The response column must contain `"upper"` and `"lower"`. Decide deliberately which coding you want: accuracy coding (upper = correct) tests selective influence, response coding (upper = one specific response) reveals decision bias. They answer different questions from the same trials.
- Bound and ndt are estimated on the log scale, and `zr` on the logit scale. The simple Censored-Shifted Wald also estimates drift on the log scale, because the drift of its single accumulator toward the correct boundary must be positive; the other approaches estimate drift on its natural scale. Back-transform with `exp()` and `plogis()` before interpreting or plotting anything, including credible-interval limits.
- `cswald(version = "simple")` reports bound on the single-boundary scale. It is the distance from the starting point to the correct boundary, half of what `ezdm`, `ddm`, and `cswald(version = "crisk")` report. Multiply by 2 before comparing it with any of them or with published values. Nothing in the output signals the difference, which makes it easy to compare two numbers that are not on the same scale.
- Parameters are defined only up to a scaling constant. `bmm` fixes the diffusion noise at $s = 1$; older software often used $s = 0.1$. Rescale published values before comparing.
- Check convergence before you interpret anything. $\hat{R}$ below 1.01 and bulk ESS above 400 for every parameter you intend to report, and no divergent transitions; `summary()` shows all three.
- Respect the trial-count minima (@tbl-model-comparison): roughly 30 per cell for the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, which needs stable variance estimates, and roughly 50 for the trial-level approaches [@lerche2017trials; @boag2025expert]. For the four-parameter version the binding quantity is the number of trials *per boundary*, because it needs an RT mean and variance for both responses in every cell: roughly 30 divided by the minority-response rate, which is about 300 trials per cell at 90% accuracy and more at higher accuracy. When accuracy is high, either accept that sparse minority boundaries enter through their response counts alone (Tutorial 2; `min_trials` sets the cutoff), or estimate $\zeta_r$ with the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald instead.
- Preprocess with the mixture tools, not with hard cutoffs. For `ezdm`, use `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")`, with one exception: four-parameter statistics for cells whose minority boundary has only a handful of responses need `method = "robust"`, because the mixture EM cannot converge on them, and `min_trials` sets how few responses a boundary may have before it enters through its counts alone; for the trial-level approaches, use `flag_contaminant_rts()` and a lower RT cutoff below any plausible non-decision time, because the trial-level likelihoods assign zero density to RTs faster than ndt (Part II).
- ndt must fall below the fastest observed RT. If ndt estimates sit suspiciously close to your minimum RT, read the Limitations section before interpreting them.

### Other Designs

The running example is a balanced within-subject design with two-level factors. The formulas carry over to other designs with two things to know. First, because `ezdm` consumes per-cell summary statistics, a predictor must be constant within a cell: factors and subject-level covariates work, whereas trial-level covariates (a continuous item property, trial number, the previous trial's response) do not and have to be binned into cells, which is what the frequency levels of Tutorial 1 are; the trial-level approaches take such predictors directly. Second, between-subject factors enter the population-level formula like any other factor but not the participant random-effects term, since a participant has only one level of them. Two examples:

```{r}
#| label: other-designs
# A three-level within-subject factor on drift (cell-means coding keeps one
# estimate per level; hypothesis() tests any contrast between them)
bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + difficulty + (0 + difficulty | id),
  bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
# A within-subject manipulation crossed with a between-subject group, plus a
# subject-level covariate (standardized working memory span) on drift
bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + load:group + span + (0 + load | id),
  bound ~ 0 + group + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

Unequal trial counts across cells need no special handling in any of the three approaches. For `ezdm`, each cell's `n_trials` enters the sampling distribution of its statistics, so sparse cells are shrunk toward the group more strongly, with the four-parameter caveats of Tutorial 2; the trial-level approaches weight every trial once.

### Inference on a Fitted `bmm` Model

Every tutorial above ran the same five steps on its fit object, and they are the steps to run on your own. The reasoning behind the last two, Savage–Dickey precision, the prior implied for a difference under cell-means coding, and when a predictive criterion is the better tool, is set out in the `bmm` hypothesis-testing vignette and in @frischkorn2026m3 [Supplement 1] and is not repeated here.

1. Convergence. `summary()` shows $\hat{R}$ and ESS for every parameter and warns about divergent transitions; `nuts_params()` counts them. Interpret nothing until $\hat{R}$ < 1.01, bulk ESS > 400, and zero divergences hold for every parameter you report.
2. Predictive checks. `pp_check()` on every observable the likelihood explains, listed by `pp_check_vars()`; for `ezdm`, `type = "intervals"` compares each design cell with its own predictive interval.
3. Estimates on the natural scale. `fixef()` returns link-scale coefficients: `exp()` for bound and ndt, `plogis()` for $\zeta_r$, and `exp()` for the drift of `cswald(version = "simple")`; multiply the simple version's bound by 2.
4. Condition effects within one fit. `hypothesis(fit, "a = b", seed = 2026)` for equalities and point nulls; read `Evid.Ratio` as the Bayes factor for the hypothesis as written, and report values at or above 10,000 as such.
5. Comparing specifications that differ in predictors or in likelihood is a different question with different tools (predictive criteria, bridge sampling) and is not part of this tutorial.

### When to Use Which Approach

The choice among the three estimation approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison) should be guided by the research question and stage of analysis:

- EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`): Best for rapid exploration and designs with many conditions. For condition effects on DDM parameters it is also a viable primary analysis in its own right, not merely a screening step, as Part I and the Cross-Approach Comparison show. Use 3par by default; 4par when starting-point bias is expected, and whether it is present is itself a point test of $\zeta_r$ = 0.5 (`zr = 0` on the logit scale) that `hypothesis()` answers from a four-parameter fit (Tutorial 2). Requires ~30 trials per cell (3par) or per boundary (4par) for stable variance estimates [@lerche2017trials; @lerche2016model].

- Censored-Shifted Wald (`cswald`): the simple version for high-accuracy data (below roughly 20% errors) when the question does not need $\zeta_r$; it is the only trial-level fit that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM (`r cost_cswald_simple` here), which is what makes iterative trial-level model development affordable, and its bound needs doubling before any comparison. The competing-risks version when errors are frequent or $\zeta_r$ is of interest, at most of the full DDM's cost (`r cost_crisk_share`% here). Part II's "When to Use Which Version" gives the reasons.

- Full DDM (`ddm`): Gold standard for confirmatory analysis. Plan for fitting times of many hours (`r cost_ddm_range` here; see @tbl-model-comparison).

These recommendations rest on a distinction worth making explicit, about what "accurate estimation" should mean in practice. Outside of simulations, the true absolute parameter values are unknown; there is no reference to recover. The criteria that carry applied work are therefore different: an estimation approach must detect differences between experimental conditions or groups, and it must separate individuals reliably [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. On both criteria the three approaches converge in our analyses; condition effects replicated across approaches (Cross-Approach Comparison), and subject-level estimates correlated highly with their generating values for all three (see the appendix). The absolute-scale biases documented above are, in this sense, primarily a theoretical rather than a practical problem; they matter when estimates are compared against published values or interpreted as measurements on an absolute scale.

### Recommended Workflow

For condition effects of DDM parameters, and for individual differences in them, fit the EZ-Diffusion Model and report it; Part I and the Cross-Approach Comparison are the case for treating it as the primary analysis. Move to a trial-level approach when the question needs what summary statistics discard: the shape of the RT distribution, trial-level predictors, cells too sparse for per-cell moments, or absolute values of bound. When you do, a staged workflow keeps the cost down. Iterating on the predictor structure is cheap with the EZ-Diffusion Model and the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), and, as the Cross-Approach Comparison showed, the faster approaches are trustworthy guides for the drift-focused questions that dominate EAM applications. Divergences that follow the patterns documented here, amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, a lower EZ-Diffusion bound, and a higher bound from the doubled simple Censored-Shifted Wald, are expected. A divergence *beyond* them, such as a reversed effect or a qualitatively different rank order, signals a potential problem (model misspecification, data-quality issues) worth investigating before you finalize the analysis.

The four stages below are for that case; when the EZ-Diffusion Model answers the question, the workflow ends at the first of them.

1. Explore and refine with the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`): Screen condition effects and settle the predictor structure, as Tutorial 1 did by moving from a two-level to a four-level stimulus contrast.

2. Develop with the Censored-Shifted Wald, simple version (`cswald`): Move to trial-level modeling here, where each iteration costs `r cost_cswald_simple` rather than `r cost_ddm_range` on data of this size. Refine the predictor structure, test different random-effects specifications, and evaluate prior sensitivity. Note that this stage is only available to you if error rates are below ~20%; above that, development has to happen at competing-risks or full-DDM cost.

3. Confirm with the full DDM (`ddm`): Fit the final model specification using the full DDM likelihood for confirmatory analysis.

4. Compare: Set the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM estimates side by side as a robustness check.

Throughout all stages, preprocess with `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")` for `ezdm` fitting (or `method = "robust"` for four-parameter statistics with sparse minority boundaries, as above) and with `flag_contaminant_rts()` plus a lower RT cutoff for trial-level fitting.

Adequate trial counts are essential for all approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison). The EZ-Diffusion Model is particularly sensitive because it relies on variance estimates, which stabilize more slowly than means [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @lerche2017trials]. For the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, @boag2025expert recommend at least 50 trials per condition for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.

### Prior Selection

All tutorials used `bmm`'s default priors, which differ between the approaches. The EZ-Diffusion Model and the full DDM place Cauchy(0, 1) on drift, Normal(0, 0.5) on bound (log link), and Normal(-1.5, 0.5) on ndt (log link). The Censored-Shifted Wald places Normal(0, 1) on drift (on the log scale in the simple version), Normal(0, 0.3) on bound and Normal(-2, 0.3) on ndt (both log link), and Normal(0, 0.3) on $\zeta_r$ in the competing-risks version (logit link). These priors are moderately informative and calibrated for typical data. Defaults can be inspected via `default_prior(formula, data, model)` and overridden using `brms::prior()`:

```{r}
#| label: priors-custom
custom_priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", dpar = "drift") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "bound")
```
